item.title: Securing Quick access from corporate networks with AWS PrivateLink
item.dc:creator: Rahul Kulkarni
item.description: Learn how to connect on-premises data sources to Amazon Quick privately with AWS PrivateLink, keeping analytics traffic off the public internet. This walkthrough covers VPC endpoints for user and API access, VPC connections for data sources, DNS and endpoint policies, identity federation, and enforcing VPC-endpoint-only access for compliance.
item.content:encoded:
When enterprise data sits behind a corporate firewall or in a private on-premises data center, there’s no direct network path from AWS, even though the AI agents and dashboards in Amazon Quick can query virtually any data source. Administrators must make sure their sensitive enterprise data isn’t exposed to the public internet while being accessible for AI-driven insights and actions.

For many enterprises, routing traffic over the public internet introduces unacceptable risk. Regulatory frameworks such as HIPAA, FedRAMP, and PCI-DSS often mandate that sensitive data remain within controlled network boundaries. Even where compliance isn’t the primary driver, exposing internal data paths increases the attack surface, complicates audit trails and introduces variable latency that can degrade the user experience.

This walkthrough shows you how to connect on-premises data sources to Amazon Quick privately, without traffic traversing the public internet. It assumes you already have AWS Direct Connect or an AWS Site-to-Site VPN linking your on-premises environment to your virtual private cloud (VPC). From that foundation, we configure VPC endpoints powered by AWS PrivateLink so that Quick can reach your private resources over the AWS backbone, then layer security groups and VPC endpoint policies for defense in depth.

By the end, you will have a network architecture that keeps traffic between Quick and your on-premises data sources off the public internet, reducing the attack surface, providing consistent low-latency connectivity, and giving you a clear audit trail for compliance.

Amazon Quick and establishing private network connectivity

Amazon Quick is an AI-powered workspace that brings search, analytics, research, and automation into a single conversational experience. Understanding which components reach your private network, and how, determines the architecture in the sections that follow.

Data access in Amazon Quick falls into two paths. User-facing traffic covers anyone opening the Quick console, interacting with a dashboard, making an API call, or using Quick Desktop. All this routes through VPC endpoints (see VPC endpoints for user and API access), keeping user sessions off the public internet.

Data-fetching traffic is when Quick itself reaches into your network to pull data. This is handled by VPC connections (see VPC connections for data source access), and it’s where most of the architectural decisions lie. The features and integrations that initiate data-fetching connections are:

  • Amazon Quick Sight queries on-premises databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle, and others) directly through ENIs placed in your VPC. This is the heaviest consumer of VPC connections.
  • Amazon Quick Flows and Amazon Quick Automate are separate automation features. Flows handle repeatable tasks. Automate handles complex, multi-system orchestration with human-in-the-loop. Both invoke action connectors, including MCP servers hosted privately in your VPC. Any workflow that calls an internal API routes through this path.
  • Quick Agents underpin all conversational interactions and can invoke action connectors directly. When a custom agent calls a privately hosted MCP server or internal API, traffic flows through the VPC connection.
  • Amazon Quick Index builds a unified search layer across connected sources such as Confluence, SharePoint, and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). For data inside your VPC or on premises, knowledge base VPC connections are currently supported only for Amazon Redshift. Sources such as Confluence, SharePoint, Box, Google Drive, OneDrive, and Amazon S3 can’t use a Quick VPC connection today (see Supported VPC data sources). You can still restrict Amazon S3 bucket access to a VPC endpoint through a bucket policy, which is a separate mechanism.
  • Amazon Quick Research accesses enterprise sources behind the firewall alongside public internet data for its citation-backed reports, using the VPC connection when reaching private sources.
  • Apps in Quick build interactive web applications on top of structured data and action connectors, inheriting the same VPC connectivity as Quick Sight and Flows.
  • Quick Spaces organize content from the preceding features but don’t initiate their own data connections.

These two traffic paths require two distinct private connectivity mechanisms that work together:

  • VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink): Handle user-facing traffic such as accessing the Quick website, making API calls, and administrative access. These keep user traffic off the public internet.
  • VPC connections: Handle data source traffic. Amazon Quick reaches into your VPC (and by extension, your on-premises network) to fetch data from databases, Amazon Redshift knowledge base sources, and internal APIs. These are configured within the Quick console.

Configuring private connectivity

This section walks through the four building blocks in order: VPC endpoints for user and API access, VPC connections for data source access, VPC endpoints for AWS data services, and outbound access to required external domains.

Prerequisites

Before configuring private connectivity for Quick, make sure the following are in place:

  • An active AWS account with an Amazon Quick Enterprise subscription (VPC connections require Enterprise edition).
  • An existing VPC in the AWS Region where Quick is deployed.
  • A supported AWS Region. Quick website VPC endpoints are not available in the AWS China Regions or the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.
  • An AWS Direct Connect connection or Site-to-Site VPN established between your on-premises network and your VPC. This is the private path that carries traffic from your data center into AWS.
  • AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to create and manage VPC endpoints, security groups, and Quick administration. To create VPC connections, the administrator’s IAM identity also needs quicksight:CreateVPCConnection, quicksight:DescribeVPCConnection, quicksight:ListVPCConnections, quicksight:UpdateVPCConnection, quicksight:DeleteVPCConnection, ec2:DescribeSubnets, ec2:DescribeVpcs, ec2:DescribeSecurityGroups, iam:ListRoles, and iam:PassRole scoped to the VPC connection execution role.
  • Access to your organization’s DNS management (Route 53 private hosted zones or on-premises DNS forwarders), as private DNS resolution routes traffic through VPC endpoints rather than public addresses.

VPC endpoints for user and API access (AWS PrivateLink)

VPC endpoints powered by PrivateLink handle all user-facing traffic to Amazon Quick, including the website, API calls, and embedded content. They prevent users from needing to traverse the public internet to access the Amazon Quick console.

Figure 1: Private access to Amazon Quick from a corporate data center through a VPC endpoint

As shown in Figure 1: (1) a client on the corporate network sends a request to Quick; (2) the request travels over AWS Direct Connect, through the Direct Connect gateway, into your VPC; (3) the Quick VPC endpoint evaluates the endpoint policy and allows or denies the request; (4) allowed requests reach Amazon Quick over the AWS network.

Planning your VPC endpoint architecture

When planning your endpoint architecture, begin by identifying the AWS Region where your Quick account is deployed, as VPC endpoints must be in the same Region. Choose subnets across multiple Availability Zones for endpoint ENI placement, and make sure those subnets have routes to your on-premises network through Direct Connect or VPN.

Design security groups that restrict traffic on the endpoint ENIs to only required ports and source ranges. If you want all traffic routed privately (including the calls Amazon Quick makes to Amazon S3, Amazon Redshift, and Amazon Athena), plan VPC endpoints for those services as well (see Configuring data source VPC endpoints).

Creating VPC endpoints for Quick

Quick requires two interface VPC endpoints for full private access:

  • Website access endpoint – Service name com.amazonaws.<region>.quicksight-website. This handles the bulk of user traffic to the Quick console. Private DNS names for the Quick website differ from the public URL, so you must create an A record for <region>.quicksight.aws.amazon.com pointing to the VPC endpoint.
  • API access endpoint – Service name com.amazonaws.<region>.quicksight. This handles programmatic API calls. When private DNS is enabled, existing API calls to quicksight.<region>.amazonaws.com automatically route through the VPC endpoint with no additional DNS configuration. For FIPS compliance, use com.amazonaws.<region>.quicksight-fips.

Note: Not every Quick API is available through the API VPC endpoint. The following 13 APIs are not supported: the action connector APIs (CreateActionConnector, DeleteActionConnector, DescribeActionConnector, DescribeActionConnectorPermissions, ListActionConnectors, SearchActionConnectors, UpdateActionConnector, UpdateActionConnectorPermissions) and the flow APIs (GetFlowMetadata, GetFlowPermissions, ListFlows, SearchFlows, UpdateFlowPermissions). Automation that manages action connectors or flows programmatically needs a path to the public API endpoint. See Quick and interface VPC endpoints.

If administrators sign in to Amazon Quick as IAM users through the VPC, also create the AWS Management Console endpoints:

  • com.amazonaws.<region>.console.
  • com.amazonaws.<region>.signin.

To create the website endpoint in the Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) console:

  1. Open the Amazon VPC console. In the navigation pane, under PrivateLink and Lattice, choose Endpoints, then choose Create endpoint.
  2. Enter a Name tag (for example, my-quicksight-vpc-endpoint) and, for Type, choose AWS services.
  3. Under Services, search for com.amazonaws.<region>.quicksight and select com.amazonaws.<region>.quicksight-website (Figure 2).

Figure 2: Naming the endpoint and selecting the Quick website endpoint service

  1. Under Network settings, select your VPC. Under Additional settings, keep Enable private DNS name selected.
  2. Select subnets in at least two Availability Zones, then select the security group for the endpoint ENIs (Figure 3).

Figure 3: Selecting the VPC, private DNS, subnets, and security group for the endpoint

  1. Choose a Policy (see the following Setting up VPC endpoint policies section), add tags, and choose Create endpoint (Figure 4).

Figure 4: Choosing the endpoint policy and creating the endpoint

  1. Repeat these steps for the API endpoint, com.amazonaws.<region>.quicksight.

Configuring DNS resolution

For the website endpoint, create an A record for <region>.quicksight.aws.amazon.com and point it to the VPC endpoint DNS name. This way, when users on your corporate network resolve the Quick URL, traffic routes through the private endpoint rather than the public internet. For the API endpoint, enabling private DNS on the VPC endpoint is sufficient, as API calls automatically resolve to the endpoint’s private IP addresses.

A Route 53 private hosted zone only answers queries from inside the VPCs associated with it. Because your users connect from the corporate network, configure your on-premises DNS servers to forward queries for <region>.quicksight.aws.amazon.com to a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint in the VPC (or host an equivalent record in your on-premises DNS). Finally, validate DNS resolution from your corporate network to confirm that requests resolve to private IPs within your VPC rather than public addresses.

To create the record in Route 53:

  1. In the Route 53 console, choose Hosted zones, then Create hosted zone.
  2. For Domain name, enter <region>.quicksight.aws.amazon.com (for example, us-east-1.quicksight.aws.amazon.com). Scoping the zone to your Region avoids overriding other Quick host names. Choose Private hosted zone, associate your VPC, and choose Create hosted zone (Figure 5).

Figure 5: Creating a private hosted zone in Amazon Route 53

  1. In the new hosted zone, choose Create record (Figure 6).

Figure 6: Creating a record in the new private hosted zone

  1. Leave Record name blank, choose record type A, turn on Alias, choose Alias to VPC endpoint, select your Region and the website endpoint’s DNS name, and choose Create records (Figure 7).

Figure 7: Creating an alias A record that points to the Quick website VPC endpoint

Setting up VPC endpoint policies

VPC endpoint policies restrict which accounts or organizations can use the endpoint. For Quick, policies can be scoped by AWS account ID or Organization ID. To change a policy, open the endpoint in the Amazon VPC console, choose the Policy tab, and choose Edit Policy (Figure 8).

Important limitation: For the Quick website endpoint, the Principal, Action, and Resource fields must all be set to *. Conditions might only be specified against the aws:PrincipalAccount or aws:OrgId attributes. More restrictive action-level policies are only supported on the API endpoint.

Website endpoint policy example:

{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Principal": "*",
            "Action": "*",
            "Resource": "*",
            "Condition": {
                "StringEquals": {
                    "aws:PrincipalAccount": ["012345678901"]
                }
            }
        }
    ]
}

Figure 8: Opening the endpoint policy from the VPC endpoint details page

API endpoint policy example (restricted to specific actions):

{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Principal": "*",
            "Action": [
                "quicksight:DescribeUser",
                "quicksight:ListUsers"
            ],
            "Resource": "*",
            "Condition": {
                "StringEquals": {
                    "aws:PrincipalAccount": ["012345678901"]
                }
            }
        }
    ]
}

Figure 9: Editing a custom VPC endpoint policy

VPC connections for data source access

While VPC endpoints handle user-facing traffic, VPC connections handle the server-side path, meaning Amazon Quick reaches into your VPC to access databases, Amazon Redshift knowledge base sources, and internal APIs.

How VPC connections work

Amazon Quick Enterprise edition is fully integrated with Amazon VPC. When you create a VPC connection in Amazon Quick, you are adding elastic network interfaces (ENIs) into your VPC subnets. These ENIs allow Quick to exchange network traffic with resources within your VPC and, by extension, anything reachable from that VPC, including on-premises systems connected through Direct Connect or VPN.

All standard VPC security controls apply to this traffic. Route tables, network ACLs, subnets, and security groups govern traffic to and from Quick in the same way they govern traffic between any other instances in your VPC. This means you can connect to:

  • Private databases not exposed to the public internet.
  • On-premises data sources reachable through Direct Connect or VPN.
  • Internal APIs accessible by IP address within your network.

Create a dedicated security group (for example, QuickSight-VPC) for the VPC connection ENIs. On each data source’s security group, allow inbound traffic on the database port from that security group ID.

Note for VPC connections created before April 27, 2023: The security group attached to the Quick network interface is not stateful. You must add an inbound rule that explicitly allows return traffic from your data source’s security group on all ports (0–65535), because return packets use randomly allocated destination ports. Connections created after that date use standard stateful behavior. See Security groups: inbound and outbound rules.

Creating the execution role

Amazon Quick doesn’t create the VPC connection execution role for you. Before you add the connection, create a dedicated IAM role (recommended), or update an existing role that already trusts Quick, such as aws-quicksight-service-role-v0 used in the screenshots in this post. The role needs:

  • A permissions policy that grants the Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) actions Quick uses to manage its ENIs (Figure 10).
  • A trust policy that allows quicksight.amazonaws.com to assume the role. Only roles with this trust policy appear in the Execution role list in the Quick console.

Permissions policy:

{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Action": [
                "ec2:CreateNetworkInterface",
                "ec2:DeleteNetworkInterface",
                "ec2:ModifyNetworkInterfaceAttribute",
                "ec2:DescribeSubnets",
                "ec2:DescribeSecurityGroups"
            ],
            "Resource": "*"
        }
    ]
}

Figure 10: Adding the Amazon EC2 permissions required by the VPC connection execution role

Trust policy:

{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Principal": { "Service": "quicksight.amazonaws.com" },
            "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
        }
    ]
}

Configuring a VPC connection

To create a VPC connection in the Quick console:

  1. Sign in to Amazon Quick as an administrator. Choose your profile icon in the upper-right, then choose Manage account (Figure 11). If you don’t see this option, you’re not a Quick administrator.

Figure 11: Opening Manage account from the Quick profile menu

  1. In the navigation pane, under Security, choose Manage VPC connections (Figure 12), then choose Add VPC connection.

Figure 12: Manage VPC connections under Security on the Manage account page

  1. Provide the following (Figure 13):
    1. A descriptive VPC connection name.
    2. The VPC ID of the target VPC. This can’t be changed later.
    3. The Execution role you created in the previous step.
    4. At least two subnets in different Availability Zones.
    5. At least one security group ID.
    6. (Optional) If your database host name must be resolved through private DNS, enter the IP addresses of your Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoints under DNS resolver endpoints.
  2. Choose ADD.

Figure 13: Adding a VPC connection in the Quick console

The connection status shows UNAVAILABLE until Quick finishes provisioning the ENIs, then changes to AVAILABLE. A status of PARTIALLY AVAILABLE means one of the ENIs is unavailable, but the connection can still be used.

Configuring data source VPC endpoints

VPC endpoints (PrivateLink, used here for AWS service APIs) and VPC connections (Quick ENIs placed in your VPC; see VPC connections for data source access) are different mechanisms. Quick accesses other AWS services (Amazon S3, Amazon Redshift, Amazon Athena, AWS Secrets Manager) when retrieving data for dashboards and analytics. If you want all traffic to remain private, including the calls Amazon Quick makes to these AWS services, create interface or gateway VPC endpoints for each:

Service Endpoint type Service name
Amazon S3 Gateway com.amazonaws.<region>.s3
Amazon Redshift Interface com.amazonaws.<region>.redshift
Amazon Athena* Interface com.amazonaws.<region>.athena
AWS Secrets Manager Interface com.amazonaws.<region>.secretsmanager
AWS Glue Interface com.amazonaws.<region>.glue

* Athena isn’t supported as a VPC connection data source. The Athena endpoint keeps Athena API traffic on AWS PrivateLink only.

Create these endpoints in the same VPC where the Amazon Quick ENIs are placed. Make sure route tables and security groups allow traffic between the Amazon Quick subnets and the endpoint subnets.

Enabling access to required external domains

While data traffic between Quick and your on-premises sources stays on the private network, users’ browsers still need to reach a set of domains for sign-in, static assets, client-side metrics, and integrations. Even with VPC endpoints configured, domains without VPC endpoint support need outbound connectivity, typically through your corporate proxy or firewall. If your account uses IAM Identity Center, browser sign-in also requires the public AWS sign-in and IAM Identity Center endpoints (see Secure user access and identity federation).

Required external domains

Domain Purpose VPC endpoint support
<region>.quicksight.aws.amazon.com Bulk of Quick website traffic Yes
quicksight.<region>.amazonaws.com Quick public API calls Yes
signin.aws.amazon.com AWS console sign-in for accounts that use IAM identities Yes
<region>.signin.aws Sign-in No
*.cloudfront.net Static assets (CSS, JavaScript) No
*.s3.<region>.amazonaws.com Reports and thumbnails Yes
*.execute-api.<region>.amazonaws.com Client-side metrics No
*.kinesisvideo.amazonaws.com Live streaming of automation workflows No
apis.google.com/js/api.js Google Drive file picker N/A
*.officeapps.live.com Quick side panel extension N/A
outlook.cloud.microsoft Quick side panel extension N/A
*.sharepoint.com Quick side panel extension N/A
*.office.com Quick side panel extension N/A
*.office365.com Quick side panel extension N/A

Source: Domains accessed by Quick.

Configuration guidance:

  • For domains with VPC endpoint support (the Quick website and API, signin.aws.amazon.com, and Amazon S3), create the corresponding VPC endpoints and DNS records.
  • For domains without VPC endpoint support, allow them through your corporate internet egress (outbound proxy or firewall). If user traffic egresses through your VPC, use a NAT gateway in a public subnet.
  • If your security posture requires URL-level filtering, use an outbound proxy or AWS Network Firewall domain filtering rules to allow only the domains listed earlier.
  • Test from a corporate workstation (or an instance in the same egress path): nslookup and curl against each domain confirm DNS resolution and routing.

Enforcing VPC endpoint restrictions

After your endpoints are configured and tested, you can enforce that all access to your Quick account must come through the VPC endpoint, blocking general internet access entirely. As a result, users can only reach Quick from your corporate network through the private path you’ve established.

Quick provides IP and VPC endpoint restriction controls that limit account access to a predefined list of IP ranges, VPC IDs, or VPC endpoint IDs. For example, you can create a rule that allows access only from the VPC endpoint used for Direct Connect, meaning anyone attempting to reach Quick from the public internet will be denied.

To configure through the Quick console (only administrators signed in with IAM credentials can access the restrictions page):

  1. Choose your profile icon, then Manage account. Under Security, choose Manage IP/VPC restrictions.
  2. In the Restriction field, enter the VPC endpoint ID (for example, vpce-001122def), enter a Description, and choose Add (Figure 14).
  3. Choose Save changes to apply the rule.
  4. Turn on Enforce restrictions.

Figure 14: Adding a VPC endpoint rule on the IP and VPC endpoint restrictions page

Alternatively, configure through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI):

aws quicksight update-ip-restriction \
--aws-account-id ACCOUNT_ID \
--region REGION \
--enabled \
--vpc-endpoint-id-restriction-rule-map \
vpce-001122def=CorporateVpcEndpoint

Note: UpdateIpRestriction replaces the entire rule map. Retrieve your current rules with aws quicksight describe-ip-restriction and include any existing rules in the update.

Key considerations:

  • IP and VPC endpoint rules apply to Quick web, embedded, and mobile access, meaning they don’t restrict access to the public API. To restrict API calls from specific sources, use IAM policies with aws:SourceIp or aws:SourceVpce conditions.
  • Make sure your own IP or VPC endpoint is included in the rules before enabling restrictions, otherwise you will lock yourself out.
  • Rules can take up to 10 minutes to take full effect.
  • You can combine IP rules and VPC endpoint rules, such that traffic is allowed if it satisfies either rule type. You can add up to 100 IP and VPC endpoint rules combined.
  • IP and VPC endpoint rules are enforced across all AWS Regions for your account, but you can only add or manage them from the AWS Region where your Quick account was created.
  • If you have publicly embedded dashboards, they will only be accessible through the VPC endpoint once restrictions are enabled.

After you enforce the restrictions, only traffic arriving through the specified VPC endpoint (or allowed IP ranges) can reach your Quick account. All other access is denied.

Secure user access and identity federation

Private network connectivity keeps traffic off the public internet, but it doesn’t answer the question of who can access what within Quick. This section covers how to integrate your corporate identity provider, control user provisioning, and enforce fine-grained access segmentation across Quick components.

Integrating with AWS IAM Identity Center

Important: For Quick accounts integrated with IAM Identity Center, browser-based authentication requires access to the public AWS sign-in and IAM Identity Center endpoints. VPC endpoints don’t provide this browser sign-in path. Public IP addresses aren’t required. Provide outbound connectivity through a NAT gateway or proxy. See Considerations for private access in the IAM Identity Center User Guide.

Amazon Quick uses AWS IAM Identity Center as the central point for workforce identity management. IAM Identity Center connects to your existing corporate identity provider (IdP) using SAML 2.0 for authentication and SCIM 2.0 for automatic user and group provisioning. This provides:

  • Automatic user provisioning and deprovisioning synced from your IdP.
  • Group membership synchronization – when a user is added to or removed from a group, that change propagates to Quick.
  • Single sign-on (SSO) using existing corporate credentials.
  • Temporary credentials through assumed IAM roles – no long-lived Quick-specific passwords.

For a step-by-step guide on setting up IAM Identity Center with your identity provider, see Getting started with IAM Identity Center.

Role-based access in Quick

Quick supports three base roles that determine what a user can do:

  • Admin – Full management access including data source configuration, VPC connections, security settings, user management, and SPICE capacity purchasing.
  • Author – Can create and publish dashboards, build agents, configure Spaces, manage data sources, create flows, and build apps.
  • Reader – Can view published dashboards, interact with agents, use Spaces they’ve been granted access to, and consume Quick Research reports.

These roles are mapped to IAM roles that federated users assume at sign-in. By managing role assignment in your IdP, you maintain a single source of truth for who has what level of access.

Additionally, Quick supports custom permissions profiles that can override default role permissions at the account, role, or user level. User-level permissions override role-level, which in turn override account-level. This gives administrators granular control beyond the three base roles.

User segmentation with Spaces

Quick Spaces provide an additional layer of access segmentation beyond roles. Each Space can be configured with specific user and group permissions, meaning:

  • A finance team Space containing sensitive revenue dashboards and financial knowledge bases is only accessible to the finance group.
  • A sales team Space with CRM-connected agents and pipeline dashboards is restricted to sales users.
  • Cross-functional Spaces can be shared across multiple groups with appropriate permissions.

Space-level access is controlled by the groups synced from your identity provider, so adding a new team member to the appropriate group automatically grants them access to the relevant Spaces.

Row-level security in Quick Sight

For dashboards backed by structured data, Quick Sight supports row-level security (RLS) that restricts which data rows each user or group can see. RLS is configured through dataset rules, which are a permissions dataset that maps users or groups to the field values they can access.

For example, a regional sales dashboard can be configured so that:

  • The EMEA sales group only sees rows where region = 'EMEA'.
  • The NA sales group only sees rows where region = 'NA'.
  • The VP of Sales sees all rows.

RLS rules are evaluated based on the user’s identity as determined by IAM Identity Center, meaning the same identity federation that controls sign-in also governs data-level access. This applies equally to traditional dashboard views and AI-powered natural language queries. The same security policies restrict what data the AI can reference when generating answers.

Column-level security

In addition to row-level restrictions, Quick Sight supports column-level security (CLS) to hide sensitive columns from specific users or groups. For example, a dataset containing employee information might restrict the salary and SSN columns to only the HR group, while other groups can still access non-sensitive columns in the same dataset.

How identity ties to private connectivity

The identity layer and network layer work together:

  1. A user on the corporate network authenticates through your IdP → IAM Identity Center → Quick.
  2. Their request reaches Quick through the VPC endpoint (the private network path; see VPC endpoints for user and API access).
  3. Quick evaluates their identity to determine role, Space access, and RLS/CLS policies.
  4. When Quick fetches data from an on-premises source, it uses the VPC connection (ENIs in your VPC; see VPC connections for data source access) to reach the database over Direct Connect.
  5. The response is returned to the user through the same private path.

Apart from the sign-in and static-asset traffic described under Enabling access to required external domains, no traffic traverses the public internet, and at every point the user’s identity determines what they can see and do.

Validation and testing

Before enforcing restrictions in production, validate end-to-end connectivity for each access pattern:

Access pattern Test Expected result
Website (VPC endpoint) nslookup <region>.quicksight.aws.amazon.com from the corporate network Resolves to a private IP in your VPC CIDR
Website (auth) Navigate to the Quick console from a corporate machine Sign-in completes via IdP. Console loads normally
API (VPC endpoint) aws quicksight describe-account-settings from within the VPC Returns account settings; Flow Logs show source IP from your VPC
Data source (VPC connection) Create a test Quick Sight data source pointing to an on-premises database through the VPC connection Connection test succeeds. Test query returns data
Knowledge base (VPC connection) Create a knowledge base from an Amazon Redshift source using the VPC connection, then trigger a sync Sync completes. Content appears in the knowledge base
Action connector (VPC connection) Create a test action pointing to an internal API and invoke it through an agent Action returns the expected response
Embedded dashboards Load an embedded Quick Sight dashboard from an internal app Dashboard renders. Browser dev tools confirm private IP

Monitoring

For ongoing visibility, enable VPC Flow Logs on all endpoint and VPC connection ENIs to capture traffic metadata. Monitor CloudWatch metrics on VPC endpoints (ActiveConnections, BytesProcessed, PacketsDropped) and set alarms for connection failures or unexpected traffic sources. These logs also serve as the audit trail referenced in your compliance documentation.

Troubleshooting common issues

Symptom Likely cause Resolution
Quick website unreachable from corporate network DNS not resolving to VPC endpoint Verify the A record for <region>.quicksight.aws.amazon.com points to the endpoint DNS name, and that on-premises DNS forwards the name to a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint. Check private DNS settings on the endpoint.
Locked out after enabling restrictions Your IP/endpoint not in the allow list Use the update-ip-restriction CLI command with an IAM identity that has API access (the API is not restricted by IP/VPC rules) to add your endpoint.
API calls timing out Security group blocking traffic Make sure the endpoint security group allows inbound HTTPS (port 443) from your corporate CIDR.
Data source connection fails VPC connection ENIs can’t reach target Verify security groups on the VPC connection ENIs allow outbound to the database port, and the database security group allows inbound from the Quick security group. For connections created before April 27, 2023, verify the inbound all-ports return-traffic rule. Check route tables for a path to the on-premises network.
Static assets not loading (blank page) External domains blocked Make sure your proxy or NAT gateway allows *.cloudfront.net, and that *.s3.<region>.amazonaws.com is reachable through an S3 VPC endpoint or your proxy.
SSO login fails Sign-in domains unreachable Allow signin.aws.amazon.com and <region>.signin.aws through your firewall/proxy. For IAM Identity Center accounts, also allow the public AWS sign-in and IAM Identity Center endpoints (see Secure user access and identity federation).
VPC connection status shows UNAVAILABLE Execution role misconfigured Verify the execution role has ec2:CreateNetworkInterface, ec2:DescribeSubnets, ec2:DescribeSecurityGroups, ec2:ModifyNetworkInterfaceAttribute, and ec2:DeleteNetworkInterface, and that its trust policy allows quicksight.amazonaws.com.
Public embedded dashboards inaccessible VPC endpoint restrictions block public traffic Known behavior: public embeds require VPC endpoint access once restrictions are enabled. Consider a separate endpoint for public consumers, or disable public embedding.

Security best practices

Neither network isolation nor identity controls alone is sufficient. This architecture relies on both: network controls prevent unauthorized access paths, while identity controls prevent unauthorized data access within authorized sessions. The practices below maintain both layers.

  • Least-privilege endpoint policies: Restrict website endpoints by aws:PrincipalAccount or aws:OrgId. On API endpoints, scope policies to only the specific actions your automation requires rather than allowing all quicksight:* actions.
  • Layered security groups: Apply security groups to both VPC endpoint ENIs (user traffic) and VPC connection ENIs (data traffic). On endpoint ENIs, restrict inbound HTTPS to your corporate CIDR ranges. On VPC connection ENIs, use a dedicated security group, restrict outbound to only the database ports and destinations Quick needs, and reference that security group in each data source’s inbound rules.
  • Enable VPC Flow Logs on all endpoint ENIs: These logs capture traffic metadata for security monitoring, anomaly detection, and compliance auditing. They also provide the audit trail that regulatory frameworks require for controlled network boundaries.
  • Audit endpoint policies regularly: Review endpoint policies quarterly. Use AWS Config rules to detect drift from your baseline configuration.
  • Separate VPC connections by sensitivity: If you have multiple data environments (dev, staging, production), create separate VPC connections with distinct security groups to prevent cross-environment access.
  • Monitor with CloudWatch: Set alarms on PacketsDropped and ActiveConnections metrics. Unusual patterns may indicate misconfiguration or attempted unauthorized access.

Example Requirements and AWS Configuration

The following examples show how the configuration in this post can address common security network requirements. Evaluate them against your own requirements with your security team.

Requirement AWS controls that can support your assessment
Sensitive data must not traverse the public internet VPC endpoints for user traffic, VPC connections for data traffic, and VPC Flow Logs for network visibility
User data isolation Security groups on VPC connection ENIs and row-level security for sensitive data access
Access restricted to authorized endpoints VPC endpoint restrictions (Section 4), CloudTrail API logs and VPC Flow Logs

Cost considerations

Component Cost model Estimate
VPC interface endpoints $0.01/hour per AZ + $0.01/GB processed ~$7.20/month per endpoint per AZ (fixed) + data transfer
VPC gateway endpoints (S3) No charge No charge
VPC connections (Quick ENIs) Included with Quick Enterprise No additional charge
NAT gateway (for external domains) $0.045/hour + $0.045/GB processed ~$32/month (fixed) + data transfer
VPC Flow Logs CloudWatch Logs ingestion rates Varies with traffic volume
Direct Connect Port hours + data transfer Varies with circuit size

Cost optimization tips:

  • Use gateway endpoints (no additional charge) for S3 instead of interface endpoints where possible.
  • Consolidate endpoint ENIs: each endpoint only needs ENIs in the AZs where the Amazon Quick VPC connection subnets reside.
  • Enable VPC Flow Logs selectively on endpoint ENIs rather than the entire VPC.
  • Consider whether all external domains need NAT gateway access or whether a targeted proxy would be more cost-effective for your traffic patterns.

Conclusion

This architecture establishes four complementary controls: VPC endpoints keep user traffic private, VPC connections give Quick a private path to your data sources, identity federation determines who can access what, and VPC endpoint restrictions make the private path mandatory. Each layer is independently auditable and maps to specific compliance requirements (see Compliance mapping).

With this in place, Quick Agents can query your on-premises databases, Quick Research can investigate enterprise sources behind the firewall, Quick Sight dashboards can visualize sensitive data, and Quick Flows can orchestrate internal systems, all without your data traversing the public internet. The AI capabilities are unchanged. The exposure is removed.

To implement, start with the VPC endpoints for user and API access, and validate user access before progressing to the VPC connections for data source access. Enable VPC endpoint restrictions only after confirming all access patterns work through the private path. For identity federation setup and advanced RLS/CLS configuration, refer to the IAM Identity Center documentation.

 

About the authors

Rahul Kulkarni

Rahul is a Generative AI and machine learning specialist at AWS, helping financial-services organizations move AI workloads from experimentation to production. He is particularly interested in how banks, investment firms, and fintechs can apply generative AI to research, customer engagement, and knowledge-intensive workflows. Outside of work, Rahul enjoys travelling and cheering on the Boston Red Sox.

Yago Tobio Souto

Yago is a Solutions Architect at AWS, based in London, specializing in generative AI, Amazon Bedrock, and agentic frameworks. He helps organizations turn AI prototypes into production-ready solutions. On weekends, he’s probably going for a run, or exploring the city… or both at the same time.

Muhammad Zain Akram

Zain is a Solutions Architect at AWS, based in Sweden, specializing in generative AI. He partners with customers to understand their business challenges and translate them into secure, scalable solutions that deliver real outcomes. In his free time, he enjoys spending time with family and friends, often over a movie or cooking food.

item.title: 5 production challenges in multi-agent systems and how Deep Insight solved them
item.dc:creator: Yoonseo Kim
item.description: Many teams build a multi-agent AI prototype in days but hit a wall in production. This post defines five production challenges (orchestration, per-agent model selection, reliable operation, secure code execution, and monitoring) and shows how Deep Insight, an open source multi-agent system on AWS, solves each.
item.content:encoded:
Building a multi-agent system is now pretty straightforward. Taking it to production is where the real challenges begin. Thanks to open source frameworks and cloud services, you can set up an agent in a matter of days. A few tool calls, a few lines of prompt, and you have something that looks impressive. But the moment teams try to move beyond a pilot and into real business applications, they hit a familiar wall. If you’ve ever tried to put an agent into production, these frustrations will sound familiar:

Why doesn’t the agent follow our business logic, skip validation steps, or catch edge cases?

You tweak the prompt, add more examples, swap out the model. The same problems keep coming back. That’s because agents don’t follow a fixed sequence of instructions. They make their own judgments based on context. Instructions alone aren’t enough. You need to design how the agent thinks, when it verifies, and what it does when things go wrong. This is exactly why it’s become critical to go beyond prompt engineering alone and design the agent’s entire cognitive architecture and execution flow.

To tackle these challenges head-on, the AWS Solutions Architecture team built Deep Insight, a production-grade multi-agent system. In this post series, we share what the team learned firsthand while building Deep Insight across three posts. We will walk through how we applied Context Engineering techniques proposed by Anthropic (multi-agent architecture, structured note-taking, human-in-the-loop, and more) in a real production environment. We also cover the trade-offs we encountered along the way (with code) and the operational insights we gained from deploying and running this agent on AWS.

Blog series overview

  • Part 1: 5 production challenges in multi-agent systems and how Deep Insight solved them.
  • Part 2: Beyond the context window: Context Engineering techniques and how Deep Insight applied them.
  • Part 3: Harness engineering in practice: moving Deep Insight from dev to production.

This is Part 1 of a three-part series. It defines the five core challenges any production multi-agent system must solve and shows how each layer of the stack addresses them, from Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Application Load Balancer, and AWS Fargate. Parts 2 and 3 cover Context Engineering and production deployment.

Introducing Deep Insight

Deep Insight is a multi-agent system that turns complex data analysis into automated insights. Given a CSV file and a natural-language prompt, a hierarchy of specialized agents (Coordinator, Planner, Supervisor, Coder, Validator, Reporter, and Tracker) collaborates on the analysis. Together they load the data, run analyses, generate charts, validate calculations, and produce a professional report (.docx) with citations.

We will explore the architecture in detail later. First, let’s see it in action. For the demo, we feed advertising data from a fictional food company, Yummy Food (yummy-food-market.csv) with a column definitions file (column_definitions.json), and provide the prompt: Analyze this from a sales and marketing perspective, generate charts and insights, and produce a .docx report. Deep Insight generates an analysis plan, presents it to the user for approval, and, once approved, executes the analysis.

 

Content
Input CSV data file (yummy-food-market.csv) + Column definitions file (column_definitions.json)
Example prompt “Analyze this from a sales and marketing perspective, generate charts and insights, and produce a .docx report.”
Output DOCX report (two versions, one with citations and one without) plus chart graphics (PNG)

The Deep Insight web demo video that follows shows the full workflow, from uploading data and reviewing the analysis plan to real-time streaming and downloading the finished report.

How can I try it?

Deep Insight is open sourced on GitHub with a full setup guide, and offers three deployment options spanning development to production.

The first is the Self-Hosted version, which runs locally through the CLI. It’s optimized for rapid iteration with full code-level access to every agent, prompt, and workflow. It sets up in about 10 minutes, which makes it well suited to development. (A Self-Hosted demo video is available on YouTube.)

The second is the Web version, a browser-based UI for uploading data, reviewing analysis plans (Human-in-the-Loop, or HITL), and downloading reports, all without writing code, making it accessible for non-developers. (The preceding demo video shows the Web version in action.)

The third is the Managed AgentCore version, a production deployment option powered by Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This version deploys the agents on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The system runs entirely within a private virtual private cloud (VPC), with a custom Code Interpreter hosted separately on AWS Fargate, and agents run concurrently in isolated per-user environments. It’s the right choice when you need session isolation and private VPC deployment. Part 3 covers its deployment and operations in detail.

All three share the same multi-agent architecture, so an agent validated in development deploys to production as-is.

Solution overview

Building a production multi-agent system takes more than good prompts. You need the right technology stack and infrastructure to address how agents collaborate, how they reason, how you deploy them, where they safely execute code, and how you monitor operational health. Deep Insight solves problems across these five key areas. Because the agents generate both code and report content, we also cover responsible AI controls for production in Solution detail 2.

Challenge Technology Approach
“How do we control execution flow across multiple agents?” Strands Agents SDK Use Strands’ Graph pattern to define execution order between agents and implement human-in-the-loop branching. Use Strands’ Agents as Tools pattern so the Supervisor can invoke specialized agents (Coder, Validator, Reporter, Tracker) as tools on demand.
“Which large language model (LLM) should each agent use?” Amazon Bedrock Select the right Claude model for each role: Haiku for basic routing, Opus for planning, Sonnet for execution.
“How do we reliably operate a finished agent in production?” Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Managed runtime with monitoring, session isolation, and private VPC deployment.
“How do we mitigate the security issues of executing AI-generated code?” AWS Fargate + Application Load Balancer (ALB) Per-session ephemeral sandbox containers for isolated code execution through a custom Code Interpreter.
“How do we monitor and manage the system?” Amazon DynamoDB + Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) + Amazon Cognito Admin dashboard and failure alerting system.

The following architecture diagram (Figure 1) illustrates this at a glance. The green boxes represent the Strands Agents multi-agent structure, which addresses challenges 1 and 2 from the preceding table. We will cover this in detail in the upcoming Solution detail 1: Multi-agent system design section. The remaining infrastructure components shown in the diagram address challenges 3, 4, and 5, which we will walk through in Solution detail 2: Production deployment and operations.

Figure 1: Solution architecture

Solution detail 1: Multi-agent system design

Deep Insight uses a multi-agent architecture in which eight agents collaborate to produce one high-quality deliverable. Each agent works in its own independent context, performs only its specialized tasks, and passes only compressed results onward.

Figure 2: Multi-agent structure

The Coordinator routes user requests, the Planner breaks tasks into discrete steps, the Plan Reviewer collects user feedback, and the Supervisor invokes the appropriate specialized agents according to the plan. The Coder writes and executes data analysis code, the Validator verifies calculations, the Reporter generates the final report, and the Tracker tracks progress. We will explain this across three layers:

  • [1st Layer] Coordinator to Planner to Plan Reviewer: Request analysis and execution plan creation.
  • [2nd Layer] Supervisor: Specialized agent orchestration.
  • [3rd Layer] Coder, Validator, Reporter, Tracker: Specialized task execution.

Two key patterns from the Strands Agents SDK are combined to control execution flow across these agents. First, the Graph pattern defines the execution order and flow of agents as a directed graph. Requests flow Coordinator, Planner, Plan Reviewer, then Supervisor, with a conditional branch looping back to the Planner on revision requests. Determining the next step by condition makes complex workflows like HITL and error handling straightforward. Second, the Agents-as-Tools pattern lets the Supervisor invoke specialized agents (Coder, Validator, Reporter, Tracker) as tools only when needed. Each works in an independent context and returns only results, minimizing context usage while preserving domain expertise.

This section shows how the architecture solves routing, planning, and orchestration.

[1st Layer] Coordinator to Planner to Plan Reviewer

This layer turns a user request into an approved execution plan.

1.1 Coordinator (routing): Not every request needs expensive orchestration

The Coordinator is the entry point for user requests. It handles basic greetings directly and routes complex tasks like data analysis to the Planner with a handoff_to_planner marker.

The key design decision is model selection: because the Coordinator only classifies, it uses the lightweight Claude Haiku, avoiding Opus-level costs on basic greetings and delivering fast responses.

# builder.py: conditional edges for routing decisions
builder.set_entry_point("coordinator")
builder.add_edge("coordinator", "planner", condition=should_handoff_to_planner)

Routing conditions come from the Coordinator’s prompt: any request needing tools, reasoning, or multi-step thinking goes to the Planner.

1.2 Planner (plan creation): Complex analyses need decomposition before execution

In Deep Insight’s multi-agent structure, the Planner agent plays the critical role of distributing tasks across agents. Before substantive work begins, it breaks large tasks into smaller steps, and each specialized agent executes them one at a time, keeping each agent’s context small.

The Planner uses a Claude Opus model with Extended Thinking turned on to develop the analysis plan. It organizes the plan into a [ ] checklist format that specifies concrete tasks assigned to each agent, stored in a full_plan variable. It breaks the request into 5–10 clear steps, as shown in the following example:

## title
Yummy Food Consumer Purchase Patterns and Advertising Effectiveness Analysis Report

## steps

### 1. Coder: Comprehensive Data Analysis and Insight Generation
- [ ] Load all data files from './data/*' path and understand structure
- [ ] Analyze consumer purchase history (patterns, preferences, customer segments)
- [ ] Analyze advertising data by channel (cost, effectiveness, channel comparison)
- [ ] Category-level analysis (fresh food, convenience food, health food ad effectiveness)
- [ ] Calculate key business metrics (conversion rate, CPA, ROAS, etc.)
- [ ] Generate visualizations (5+ charts, consumer segment charts)
- [ ] Derive strategic marketing insights
- [ ] Generate calculation metadata (for validation)

### 2. Validator: Calculation Verification and Citation Metadata Generation
- [ ] Identify verification targets and extract filter calculations
- [ ] Load data files directly and perform recalculations
- [ ] Verify accuracy of per-channel performance metrics
- [ ] Validate data consistency of visuals and graphs
- [ ] Generate citation metadata (reference numbers for verified items)

### 3. Reporter: Marketing Analysis Report Generation
- [ ] Write report overview
- [ ] Create structured report using verified analysis results
- [ ] Insert visualizations and analysis sections
- [ ] Present marketing strategy recommendations and improvement proposals
- [ ] Generate professional marketing report in DOCX format

1.3 Plan Reviewer

The Plan Reviewer is a HITL node that presents the plan to the user and collects approval or revision feedback. If there is feedback, it loops back to the Planner to revise the plan. If approved, it hands the task off to the Supervisor. A maximum revision count (MAX_PLAN_REVISIONS) is set to prevent infinite loops.

# builder.py: Plan Reviewer's bidirectional conditional edges
builder.add_edge("plan_reviewer", "planner", condition=should_revise_plan)
builder.add_edge("plan_reviewer", "supervisor", condition=should_proceed_to_supervisor)
builder.set_max_node_executions(25)

In the Web version, the Plan Reviewer shows a browser modal where the user reads the plan and approves it or enters revision feedback. A 300-second countdown auto-approves the plan if no response arrives.

Figure 3: Plan Reviewer agent execution in the web UI

Without planning, the agent decides everything at runtime, a mid-course correction invalidates previous work, and users have no visibility into progress. With the Planner and Plan Reviewer, the user can review and revise the plan, monitor progress in real time, and re-execute only a failed step.

[2nd Layer] Supervisor (orchestrator): Specialized agents need a conductor

The Supervisor executes the Planner’s full_plan in order, invoking the Layer 3 agents (Coder, Validator, Reporter, Tracker) as tools registered on it through Tool Use.

# nodes.py: registering sub-agents as tools on the Supervisor
agent = strands_utils.get_agent(
    agent_name="supervisor",
    system_prompts=apply_prompt_template(prompt_name="supervisor", prompt_context={}),
    model_id=os.getenv("SUPERVISOR_MODEL_ID", os.getenv("DEFAULT_MODEL_ID")),
    prompt_cache_info=(True, "default"),
    tool_cache=True,
    tools=[coder_agent_tool, reporter_agent_tool, tracker_agent_tool, validator_agent_tool],
    streaming=True,
)

The Supervisor’s system prompt defines strict workflow rules:

  • Mandatory execution order: Coder, Tracker, Validator, Tracker, Reporter, Tracker: after each agent runs, Tracker is invoked to track progress, letting the Supervisor manage overall task state.
  • Section completion rule: The Supervisor does not move to the next agent until all checklist items for the current agent are marked [x].
  • Context preservation: The Supervisor passes clues and full_plan variables to each tool agent, maintaining full context and preventing information loss.

[3rd Layer] Coder, Validator, Reporter, Tracker: Division of labor drives quality

Each Layer 3 agent (Coder, Validator, Reporter, Tracker) is wrapped as a PythonAgentTool and receives Tool Use calls from the Supervisor. Each is created as an independent Agent() instance in the Strands SDK with its own system prompt, model ID, and toolset.

Agent Role Tools Key Output
Coder Data analysis, chart generation, insight derivation write_and_execute_tool, bash_tool, file_read, skill_tool *.png charts, calculation_metadata.json
Validator Numerical calculation re-verification, citation generation write_and_execute_tool, bash_tool, file_read citations.json, validation_report.txt
Reporter DOCX report generation write_and_execute_tool, bash_tool, file_read final_report.docx, final_report_with_citations.docx
Tracker Checklist progress status updates None (LLM reasoning only) Updated full_plan

The Supervisor invokes Tool Use calls in this order, based on the Planner’s checklist:

  1. Coder – Loads data, writes and runs analysis code, produces PNG charts, accumulates results in all_results.txt, and leaves calculation_metadata.json for verification.
  2. Tracker (1st pass) – Updates completed checklist items from [ ] to [x], which the Supervisor uses to decide whether to proceed.
  3. Validator – Re-performs each calculation in calculation_metadata.json from the source data. Matches within 0.01 pass, mismatches are flagged. Verified calculations go to citations.json for the Reporter to cite.
  4. Tracker (2nd pass) – Reflects the Validator’s completion status in the checklist.
  5. Reporter – Reads all_results.txt and citations.json to generate the final DOCX report in two versions, with and without citations.
  6. Tracker (3rd pass) – Reflects the final completion status of all tasks.

Tracker runs after every agent so the Supervisor can track progress and enforce the completion rule (no moving on until all items are [x]). Because it updates the checklist with LLM reasoning and no tools, it adds little overhead.

Per-agent LLM model configuration

Deep Insight tailors the model and settings to each agent’s role. This isn’t a model selection. It’s an architectural decision to optimize cost and quality.

Agent Model Extended Thinking Prompt Caching Role
Coordinator Haiku Disabled No Fast routing: cost minimization
Planner Opus Enabled (~8,192 tokens) No Deep thinking: high-quality planning
Supervisor Sonnet Disabled Yes Execution orchestration: caching for cost savings
Coder Sonnet Disabled Yes Code generation/execution: caching effective for repeated calls
Validator Sonnet Disabled No Numerical verification: different data each time, caching unnecessary
Reporter Sonnet Disabled Yes Report generation: caching effective for long prompts
Tracker Sonnet Disabled No Status updates: lightweight tasks, caching unnecessary

The Supervisor, Coder, and Reporter agents use Prompt Caching to cache their system prompts and tool definitions, reducing input token costs by up to 90 percent on repeated calls. The Coordinator runs only once, and the Validator and Tracker run with different contexts each time, so caching is ineffective for them and stays disabled. This selective caching strategy is a deliberate cost/performance trade-off.

Solution detail 2: Production deployment and operations

If Solution detail 1 defined what the system does, this section defines where and how it runs safely. Everything from here on covers infrastructure decisions for production operations. Specifically, this section covers the secure execution environment for LLM-generated code, and operational visibility for the team.

1. Code execution: LLM-generated code needs a secure execution environment

The Coder agent writes and runs Python for data analysis. In the Self-Hosted version it runs locally through subprocess.run(), but in production (AgentCore) security and isolation are essential. Running LLM-generated code directly on a production server is risky: the model might delete system files, exhaust resources in an infinite loop, or reach other users’ analysis data. Deep Insight solves this with per-session ephemeral containers on AWS Fargate and ALB. These components don’t run in isolation. As shown in Figure 1, AgentCore runtime, the ALB, and the Fargate tasks all run inside the same private VPC. VPC endpoints connect them to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Amazon Bedrock, and Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) without traversing the public internet. Security groups restrict which components can reach the Code Interpreter containers. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles scope each component to only the AWS resources it needs. Amazon CloudWatch collects container logs and observability data from AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

  • Custom container Docker image: A pre-optimized sandbox with fonts, system libraries, and Python packages for the multi-agent system.
  • Container isolation: Each analysis session gets an independent Fargate container in a private VPC subnet with no direct internet access.
  • 2-step execution: LLM-generated code is base64-encoded, sent over HTTP, written to a file (Step 1), then executed through subprocess (Step 2).
  • Session affinity: ALB sticky session cookies route an agent back to the same container even when it executes code multiple times.
  • Artifact management: Charts, reports, and logs upload to Amazon S3 when analysis completes. Containers terminate automatically after one hour.

Container isolation protects the infrastructure, but it doesn’t govern what the agents generate. The Validator agent re-verifies calculations. It doesn’t detect prompt-injection instructions hidden in uploaded data or screen LLM-generated text for harmful or ungrounded content. For production deployments, we recommend adding Amazon Bedrock Guardrails as a responsible AI control: apply content filters and prompt attack detection to user prompts and uploaded data, and apply contextual grounding checks to agent outputs so that report text stays grounded in the source data and verified calculations.

2. Operations and monitoring: Teams need visibility

A production system isn’t complete with code alone. The team must assess system health, diagnose issues, and review results, so Deep Insight provides a Web UI and an Ops dashboard.

Web UI (deep-insight-web)

A FastAPI-based web interface that communicates with the backend through the AgentCore Native Protocol (boto3.invoke_agent_runtime()). Users upload data and enter a prompt, then monitor progress through Server-Sent Events (SSE) streaming. When the plan is generated, a modal lets the user approve or give revision feedback (HITL). The finished report can be downloaded directly. Both Korean and English are supported.

Figure 4: Deep Insight web version screenshot

Ops dashboard (deep-insight-web/ops)

The Ops dashboard is optional. Deep Insight works fine without it, but it adds these features for teams that need them:

  • Task tracking: All analysis task metrics, including status, token usage, and elapsed time, are recorded in Amazon DynamoDB.
  • Failure alerting: When an analysis fails, an email is immediately sent to administrators through Amazon SNS.
  • Admin dashboard: A dedicated admin dashboard is protected by JSON Web Token (JWT) authentication through Amazon Cognito for secure task monitoring.

Figure 5: Deep Insight Ops dashboard screenshot

Figure 6: Deep Insight Ops dashboard detail view

Extending the Deep Insight architecture

Deep Insight’s multi-agent architecture isn’t confined to the single domain of data analysis report generation. The following two examples demonstrate that the hierarchical orchestration design principles remain effective in entirely different domains.

Case 1: LG Electronics: Agentic AI-powered marketing insight extraction system

LG Electronics’ Korea Sales Division built ChatInsight on the same multi-agent architecture as Deep Insight, where data analysis requests had taken 2–3 weeks and lost intent between marketers and data scientists. The Coordinator routes by complexity, the Planner tracks tasks, and the Supervisor orchestrates the Coder and Reporter, with inter-agent state passed cumulatively through an all_results.txt file. Analysis that took 3 days now takes 30 minutes, a 288x productivity improvement. Marketers who don’t know SQL can let the agent explore data and propose strategies (see the LG Electronics Agentic AI Insight Extraction System on the AWS Tech Blog).

Figure 7: LG Electronics Agentic AI marketing insight system architecture

Case 2: TechRecon: AI-powered technology reconnaissance agent (re:Invent 2025)

Presented at AWS re:Invent 2025 (session SNR203), TechRecon applies Deep Insight’s architecture to technology strategy. Given a company and sector, a Researcher gathers technology trends, the Coder analyzes, the Validator verifies, and the Reporter produces a Landscape Analysis and a Technical Position Paper. The architecture is nearly identical to Deep Insight, built with the Strands Agents SDK Graph pattern and Extended Thinking and Prompt Caching, with Researcher replacing Coder as the primary execution agent. It shows the design is a general-purpose pattern: swap the agents’ roles and prompts, and the same orchestration structure solves entirely different problems.

Figure 8: TechRecon results

(Read more: TechRecon GitHub | AWS re:Invent Session Video)

Conclusion

Building an agent that works in production is not a matter of model capability. It’s a matter of architecture. Deep Insight offers a proven answer:

  • Workflow management: The Strands Agents SDK’s Graph pattern defines execution order between agents and implements HITL branching, while the Agents-as-Tools pattern lets the Supervisor invoke specialized agents only when needed.
  • Reasoning engine: We assign Claude models from Amazon Bedrock by role (Haiku, then Opus, then Sonnet) to optimize cost and quality.
  • Deployment: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides a managed runtime with session isolation, private VPC deployment, and OpenTelemetry observability.
  • Code execution: Application Load Balancer plus Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on Fargate isolates LLM-generated code execution in per-session ephemeral sandbox containers, preventing security issues such as system file access, resource exhaustion, and unintended data disclosure.
  • Operations: The Web UI’s SSE streaming and the Ops dashboard (DynamoDB + Cognito + SNS) provide visibility across the entire team.

LG Electronics’ marketing insight system and the TechRecon case at re:Invent 2025 validated these design principles.

In Part 2, we examine four layers of Context Engineering techniques for overcoming context-window limits on top of this architecture, from architecture-level isolation to prompt design, tool optimization, and verification safeguards, comparing our approach with Anthropic’s engineering research.

Deep Insight is open source. Explore the code and extend it for your own domain.

  • GitHub
  • Workshop: Deep Insight Workshop (English | Korean)

Kyutae, Ph.D. is an AI Specialist Solutions Architect who helps customers across industries design and build applied AI workloads, drawing on extensive experience in machine learning, MLOps, and agentic AI. He focuses on intelligent automation and operational innovation through agentic AI, bringing autonomous decision-making and multi-agent collaboration architectures into real-world business environments. Through this work, he helps customers use AWS AI/ML services and applied generative AI to achieve tangible business outcomes and build a sustainable competitive advantage.

item.title: Adaptive agentic intelligence framework using Strands Agents
item.dc:creator: Nitin Eusebius
item.description: The Adaptive Agentic Intelligence Framework (AAIF), built with Strands Agents, handles routine tasks locally with small language models and routes complex requests to cloud models through Amazon Bedrock. This post walks through building AAIF with local SLMs through Ollama and Amazon Bedrock, using an Internet of Things monitoring scenario.
item.content:encoded:
Organizations building AI agents face a common challenge: Every request, whether a routine status check or complex analysis, typically gets routed to a single large, expensive model. This one-size-fits-all approach can drive up API costs, introduce unpredictable latency, and remove the possibility of offline operation. Even routine queries that could resolve locally end up requiring a full network round-trip to a cloud-hosted large language model (LLM).

The Adaptive Agentic Intelligence Framework (AAIF), built with Strands Agents, takes a different approach. Instead of routing all requests to a single large model, AAIF uses small language models (SLMs) to handle routine tasks locally. More complex requests are routed to cloud-hosted models through Amazon Bedrock. This approach builds on the research position from Belcak et al. at NVIDIA. They argue that small language models are “sufficiently powerful, inherently more suitable, and necessarily more economical for many invocations in agentic systems.” Built on Strands Agents, the framework demonstrates how intelligent model orchestration can help reduce costs while maintaining low latency for local operations.

In this post, we walk through the key components of AAIF using Strands Agents with local SLMs through Ollama and cloud models through Amazon Bedrock. We use an Internet of Things (IoT) monitoring scenario as a reference implementation.

Solution overview

AAIF organizes AI processing into three layers, each optimized for different task types, as Figure 1 shows:

  1. Smart orchestration uses a lightweight SLM (llama3.2:1b) as the decision-making layer. This orchestrator classifies incoming requests and routes them to the appropriate processing layer without hardcoded rules.
  2. Local processing handles routine tasks like device telemetry retrieval and image analysis using SLMs running on local hardware through Ollama. These tasks complete with low latency and no cloud dependency.
  3. Cloud processing handles complex pattern analysis and strategic recommendations through frontier models in Amazon Bedrock. These requests need broader context and multi-step reasoning that SLMs cannot reliably provide.

Figure 1: The three AAIF processing layers for smart orchestration, local processing, and cloud processing

Figure 1 shows the complete AAIF system architecture. At the center sits the Strands agent, which connects to an Ollama runtime hosting both the 1B-parameter orchestrator model and the vision model. The agent exposes three tools: get_device_telemetry for local sensor data retrieval, analyze_camera_feed for on-device vision processing through llama3.2-vision, and get_expert_insights which calls Amazon Bedrock through boto3 for complex analysis. Incoming user requests flow through the SLM orchestrator, which classifies each request and dispatches it to either a local tool or the cloud endpoint based on task complexity.

Figure 2: Complete AAIF system architecture showing the Strands agent, Ollama runtime, tool integrations, and Amazon Bedrock connectivity

The framework adapts to your deployment constraints rather than requiring you to restructure your infrastructure around it. This architecture runs on edge devices like a Raspberry Pi with 8 GB of memory, in full cloud deployments where all inference hits Amazon Bedrock, or in hybrid configurations that combine local speed with cloud reasoning. The flexibility comes from separating the routing logic (the SLM orchestrator) from the processing tools, which you can swap or reconfigure independently depending on available hardware and network connectivity.

Prerequisites

For this walkthrough, you should have the following prerequisites:

  • An AWS account.
  • Amazon Bedrock model access configured in the required Region.
  • Python 3.10+ installed.
  • Ollama installed with the following models pulled:
    • ollama pull llama3.2:1b (orchestrator).
    • ollama pull llama3.2-vision (vision analysis).
  • Strands Agents installed: pip install strands-agents strands-agents-tools.
  • AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) configured with appropriate credentials.
  • Boto3 installed: pip install boto3.

Set up the environment

Create a project directory and start the Ollama server:

mkdir aaif-demo && cd aaif-demo
ollama serve

Pull the required models:

ollama pull llama3.2:1b
ollama pull llama3.2-vision

Create a file called aaif_agent.py and add the following components.

Implement local processing tools

Strands Agents uses the @tool decorator to define capabilities that agents can invoke. Start by creating tools for local processing.

The first tool retrieves device telemetry data. In a production environment, this would connect to actual IoT sensors. For this walkthrough, it uses simulated device data:

from strands import Agent, tool
import random

DEVICE_TELEMETRY = {
    "sensor-001": {
        "device_type": "Temperature Sensor",
        "location": "Building A - Floor 2",
        "temperature": 72.5,
        "humidity": 45.2,
        "status": "normal"
    },
    "camera-001": {
        "device_type": "Security Camera",
        "location": "Main Entrance",
        "fps": 30,
        "resolution": "1080p",
        "status": "recording"
    },
    "hvac-001": {
        "device_type": "HVAC Controller",
        "location": "Building A - Central",
        "set_temp": 71.0,
        "current_temp": 72.5,
        "mode": "cooling",
        "status": "active"
    }
}

@tool
def get_device_telemetry() -> str:
    """Retrieve current telemetry data from connected IoT devices."""
    device_id = random.choice(list(DEVICE_TELEMETRY.keys()))
    device_data = DEVICE_TELEMETRY[device_id]

    report = f"Device: {device_id} ({device_data['device_type']})\n"
    report += f"Location: {device_data['location']}\n"
    report += f"Status: {device_data['status']}\n"
    for key, value in device_data.items():
        if key not in ['device_type', 'location', 'status']:
            report += f"{key}: {value}\n"
    return report

The second tool performs vision analysis using a local SLM. The llama3.2-vision model runs entirely on local hardware, which means sensitive camera feeds don’t leave the device:

import ollama

@tool
def analyze_camera_feed(image_path: str) -> str:
    """Analyze visual data from cameras using local vision model."""
    stream = ollama.chat(
        model='llama3.2-vision',
        messages=[{
            'role': 'user',
            'content': 'Describe this image in one sentence. '
            'What are the 3 most important things you see?',
            'images': [image_path]
        }],
        stream=True,
    )

    full_response = ""
    for chunk in stream:
        chunk_content = chunk['message']['content']
        print(chunk_content, end='', flush=True)
        full_response += chunk_content

    return f"Object Detection Report:\n{full_response}"

Implement cloud processing

For complex analysis that requires broader reasoning, create a tool that calls Amazon Bedrock. This tool is invoked only when the orchestrator determines that local models can’t handle the request:

import boto3

@tool
def get_expert_insights(context_data: str, question: str) -> str:
    """Get advanced analysis and expert recommendations
    for complex questions via Amazon Bedrock."""
    client = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="us-east-1")

    conversation = [
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {"text": f"Context: {context_data}\n\nQuestion: {question}"}
            ],
        }
    ]

    response = client.converse(
        modelId="<<model_id>", //Refer model id [details](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/foundation-models-reference.html)
        messages=conversation,
        inferenceConfig={
            "maxTokens": 512,
            "temperature": 0.5,
            "topP": 0.9
        }
    )

    response_text = response["output"]["message"]["content"][0]["text"]
    return f"Expert Analysis:\n{response_text}"

Configure the Strands agent with smart orchestration

The core of AAIF is the Strands agent configuration. The agent uses a local SLM (llama3.2:1b) as its orchestrator. Strands Agents supports multiple model providers, and here we use the Ollama provider to run the orchestrator locally:

from strands.models.ollama import OllamaModel

model = OllamaModel(
    model_id="llama3.2:1b",
    host="http://localhost:11434",
    params={
        "max_tokens": 300,
        "temperature": 0.3,
    },
)

system_prompt = """You are a monitoring assistant for operational facilities.
You have access to device telemetry tools, analysis capabilities,
and expert insights to help monitor operations effectively.

When users ask for:
- Device status or telemetry: use get_device_telemetry
- Image or data analysis: use analyze_camera_feed
- Expert advice or complex questions: use get_expert_insights

Always return the complete tool results directly to the user."""

agent = Agent(
    model=model,
    system_prompt=system_prompt,
    tools=[
        get_device_telemetry,
        analyze_camera_feed,
        get_expert_insights,
    ],
)

The SLM-powered orchestrator analyzes each request and routes it to the appropriate tool without hardcoded keyword matching. The routing happens through the model’s understanding of the request:

Request Routing Latency
“Check device status” Local SLM Low (local inference)
“Analyze this image” Local vision AI Low (local inference)
“What optimization strategies do you recommend?” Cloud (Amazon Bedrock) Higher (network round-trip)

Table 1: Request, routing, and latency estimates for local compared to cloud inference

Run the agent

With the agent configured, you can interact with it directly:

# Local processing - device telemetry
response = agent("What's the current status of our devices?")
print(response)

# Local processing - vision analysis
response = agent("Analyze the camera feed from camera-001")
print(response)

# Cloud processing - complex analysis
response = agent(
    "Based on current telemetry patterns, "
    "what optimization strategies do you recommend?"
)
print(response)

The agent automatically classifies each request and routes it to the appropriate processing layer. No explicit routing rules are needed.

Adapt to different deployment scenarios

The AAIF architecture adapts to different infrastructure requirements by changing the model configuration:

When your workload runs entirely in the cloud and no edge hardware is available, replace the Ollama model configuration with Amazon Bedrock for all processing. This routes every request through managed cloud inference, giving you auto scaling without requiring local GPU resources. Teams with reliable low-latency connectivity and no data residency constraints benefit most from this configuration:

from strands.models import BedrockModel

model = BedrockModel(
    model_id="<<model_id>", //Refer model id [details](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/foundation-models-reference.html)
    region_name="us-east-1"
)

The hybrid configuration keeps the local SLM orchestrator intact while adding cloud models for requests that exceed local model capabilities. This is the default AAIF configuration shown in this walkthrough. It suits environments where most requests are routine enough to resolve locally, but some require the broader reasoning of a larger model. Cost savings can come from the roughly 80 percent of traffic that doesn’t hit a paid API endpoint.

For environments that are fully air-gapped or have strict data sovereignty requirements, replace the cloud tool with a larger local model and run all processing on-device. A 3B-parameter model running on hardware with adequate memory can handle moderately complex tasks that the 1B orchestrator would otherwise escalate. The trade-off is reduced reasoning depth on the hardest queries, but the benefit is data not leaving the premises:

model = OllamaModel(
    model_id="llama3.2:3b", # Larger local model for complex tasks
    host="http://localhost:11434",
)

Looking ahead: Centralized tool calling with MCP servers

The implementation in this post uses local tool calls defined directly in the agent code. For production deployments with multiple agents sharing tools across services, expose these tools as Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.
