Figure 6: The uniform AgentCore control set before the backend (IAM auth, per-tool authorization, input validation, policy evaluation, rate limiting, data-boundary enforcement, audit logging)

The MCP servers in this pattern

MCP server Capabilities Example queries
Quoting Engine (sc-quoting-gateway) Quote generation, pricing rules, validation “Contract-aligned quote for 500 units of SKU-A”
Governance Engine (sc-governance-gateway) Supplier approval, budget authority, regulatory compliance, policy rules “Is SupplierCo on our approved vendor list?”
Invoice Processing (sc-invoice-gateway) Invoice approval routing, AP aging, payment schedules “What invoices are pending approval this week?”
Disruption Alerts (sc-disruption-alert-gateway) Active disruptions, severity, impact assessments, mitigation “Critical disruptions affecting our APAC suppliers?”
Order Fulfillment Agent (sc-order-fulfillment-agent) Multi-step orchestration across all four business MCPs (AgentCore Runtime, direct invocation URL) “A supplier went down, find alternatives, check compliance, issue an RFQ”

Amazon Quick: The enterprise AI assistant

Amazon Quick puts AgentCore tools before business users through chat, agents, the Activity Feed, and automated workflows, with no technical setup.

Key components used

Component Role in this pattern How it works
Agent Registry connection Surfaces MCP servers as connectors Admin links the registry once. Records become connector cards
Quick Agent One SC agent that adapts to role Tailors to persona (manager, procurement, analyst)
MCP connectors Expose MCP tools in chat A card connector exposes tools across Chat, agents, schedules
Activity Feed Proactive alerts and actions Agents post cards. The user acts
Schedules Recurring natural-language automation For example, “every morning”
Outlook Integration Email into the feed Supplier replies parsed and validated
Structured data connectors Query operational records Quick queries Space datasets (orders, inventory, suppliers, contracts) for the MCP rule check
Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) knowledge base Retrieval over documents Invoices, contracts, policies in an S3 knowledge base, grounding answers through Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)
CRM connector (optional) Reads customer records (optional) CRM (for example, Salesforce) accounts, opportunities, contacts. Can also load into datasets

Automated Activity Feed and proactive monitoring

The Activity Feed is the proactive surface of Amazon Quick, a unified inbox where agents post results, alerts, and recommendations. Feed items are:

  • Actionable, each carries context and next-step actions.
  • AI-triaged, with priority indicators (Reply needed, Follow up, Deadline).
  • Cross-source, spanning email, schedules, agent runs, and external systems.
  • Human-in-the-loop, where agents propose and humans decide.

How automated monitoring works

AgentCore tools plus the proactive capabilities of Amazon Quick give two paths, time-based and email-driven, through a common trigger → agent → output pipeline.

Figure 7: Three-stage pipeline from trigger (schedule or email) to autonomous agent (assess_disruption_impact, check_supplier_approval, apply_approval_rules, validate_quote) to review-ready card

Use case: Validate supplier responses from email

Suppliers reply to an emergency RFQ by email with pricing. The agent validates each (approved supplier? within guidelines?) and stages the result. It does not author a quote, pick a winner, or issue a purchase order (PO).

Phase 1: Setup (one-time, approximately 5 minutes)

  1. Connect Outlook: in Amazon Quick, choose Settings → Connections → Add Outlook.
  2. Configure Activity Feed: turn on email monitoring in feed preferences.
  3. Create SC Agent: build an agent with these instructions:
Supply chain procurement assistant. On a supplier RFQ reply with pricing: 1) extract SKU(s), quantities, pricing; 2) validate approved vendor (Governance MCP); 3) check pricing within guidelines (Quoting MCP); 4) post a review-ready card (approved-supplier, within-guidelines); do NOT draft a PO or select a supplier.
  1. Create Schedule: “Every 2 hours during business hours, check for new supplier replies and validate them.”

Phase 2: Runtime (fully automated)

Schedule -> email from "TechSupply Co" (MCU-7200, 10,000 units @ $2.45/unit) -> Governance MCP: approved? | Quoting MCP: within guidelines? -> "Supplier Response - Ready for Review" card

The feed card carries the validation results and decision-relevant facts:

Supplier Response: Ready for Review Details
Supplier TechSupply Co, approved vendor
SKU / Qty / Price MCU-7200 · 10,000 units · $2.45/unit
Price check within purchasing guidelines
Actions Select for PO · Compare responses · Reject

Phase 3: Human-in-the-loop

The reviewer compares validated responses and either selects a supplier and issues the PO, or rejects with a logged reason. Selection and the PO stay with a person.

Use case: Proactive disruption monitoring

Schedule-triggered, the same pattern applies: a daily 8:30 AM agent checks for new critical or high-severity disruptions, assesses impact, flags anything under seven days of supply as URGENT, and posts an alert card with an Issue Emergency RFQ action.

Where this fits alongside traditional BI

Dimension Traditional business intelligence (BI) / dashboards AgentCore + Amazon Quick
Access model Navigate, log in, find the dashboard/report Ask in natural language. The system finds the source
Time to insight Minutes to hours (find → filter → export → correlate) Seconds (ask → answer with cross-system context)
Multi-system correlation Manual: 3-4 tabs, copy-paste Automatic: the agent orchestrates across MCP servers from one query
Action gap Insight in one tool → switch → act in another Insight → action in the same conversation
Setup cost Weeks/months (dashboard design, ETL, permissions, training) Minutes to connect, once your MCP servers exist
Run cost Fixed: pipelines cost the same whether or not anyone asks Usage-based: serverless scales to zero, cost tracks questions (Lambda + agent tokens)
Trust & accuracy As fresh as the last ETL load Computed live from systems of record and grounded docs, every write human-gated

This isn’t a “replace everything” argument. Dashboards remain superior for trend visualization, collaborative analysis, regulatory reporting, and exploratory analysis. Use conversational AI for real-time operational decisions and BI for strategic analysis. They complement, not compete.

Personas and use cases

One Quick Agent serves all three personas: the manager maintains continuity, procurement sources with compliance-awareness, the analyst correlates signals. Persona also bounds reach, through row/column-level security and per-persona MCP-tool scoping, so procurement does not see finance data.

Persona Use case Tools invoked Outcome
SC Manager Morning disruption check Disruption Alerts MCP Disruptions, revenue at risk, days of supply
SC Manager Emergency procurement Governance → Quoting MCP Verified alternatives + RFQ, one flow
Procurement Supplier verification, budget authority Governance MCP Approval, compliance, limits
Procurement RFQ generation and response validation Quoting MCP RFQ issued + responses validated
Ops Analyst Cross-system correlation SC Operations Agent Multi-MCP reasoning, one query
Ops Analyst Payment queue, audit, disruption trends Invoice / Governance MCP AP aging, audit log, patterns

Getting started

Deploying the pattern takes three phases: provision the infrastructure, connect Amazon Quick to your data and the registry, and turn on monitoring.

Prerequisites

Before you begin:

  • An AWS account with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and AWS Agent Registry.
  • AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) v2, AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM) CLI, and Docker (the agent runs as an arm64 container).
  • Python 3.12 or later, with Boto3 1.43.94 or later for the registry step.
  • Active credentials with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to deploy and register (aws sts get-caller-identity returns the target account).
  • Data layer: a database (Snowflake, PostgreSQL/RDS, or a SQLAlchemy engine), an Amazon S3 bucket, optionally a Salesforce org.
  • Amazon Quick set up for your organization.
  • (Optional) An Outlook account for email automation.

Setup uses two surfaces, so each of the following steps names where it happens: the Amazon Quick web console in a browser (Amazon Quick Sight permissions, Agent Registry linking, connectors, and agent settings) and the Quick Desktop App (connecting Outlook for email automation). The conversational experience in the Desktop App comes last, once setup is done.

Deploy the infrastructure

Everything is open source and scripted: clone the quick-for-supply-chain example in the aws-samples/sample-amazon-quick-suite-knowledge-hub repository and follow its README.md, or point a coding agent like Kiro at it.

The README.md covers three phases. Phase 1 deploys the AgentCore stack: the identity layer (an Amazon Cognito user pool and app client, authorization-code OAuth flow, plus a test user), four business-rule MCP servers (each an AWS Lambda function fronted by its own AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, using CUSTOM_JWT authorization), the gateway targets mapping the tools of each Lambda function, and sc-order-fulfillment-agent on AgentCore Runtime as a container, with least-privilege IAM roles. Phase 2 uploads the synthetic dataset to Amazon S3. Phase 3 verifies gateways and runtime are Ready. Six Agent Registry records are approved.

Figure 8: AWS Agent Registry console with six approved records (four MCP Server, one Agent, one Skills)

Grant Amazon Quick access to your data

In the Amazon Quick web console (browser): grant Amazon Quick access from the Amazon Quick Sight admin page (Manage Quick Sight → Security and permissions) to both the S3 bucket and Amazon Athena, since each table is served through an Athena source over an AWS Glue database. Without the Athena grant, dataset creation fails.

Figure 9: Amazon Quick Sight Security and permissions, with Amazon Athena alongside Amazon S3

Link the registry and create connectors

Linking the registry is one-time and administrator-level. Creating a connector is per-user. Both happen in the Amazon Quick console. See the AWS Agent Registry integration guide.

Link the registry (administrator, one-time)

An administrator links one Agent Registry to the Quick account. In the Amazon Quick web console (admin): go to Manage account → Permissions → AWS Agent Registry and turn on the registry (sc-supply-chain-registry, one per account). Only registries in your account and Region, agent-registry namespace, AWS_IAM (SigV4) authorization, and READY status appear. The Quick-managed service role links it.

Figure 10: Linking the registry, where only READY, AWS_IAM registries are selectable

Create a connector

After the registry is linked, approved MCP server records become connector cards: the four business MCPs as cards, the order-fulfillment agent added manually. At scale, federate connector authentication through your identity provider and provision connectors to groups, with the Cognito user pool as the seam.

In the Amazon Quick web console (per user): the four cards appear on the Connectors page (sc-quoting-mcp, sc-governance-mcp, sc-invoice-processing-mcp, sc-disruption-alert-mcp). Authenticate through the OAuth authorization-code flow (OAUTH2_AUTHORIZATION_CODE) with client ID, secret, and token, authorization, and redirect URLs from the deploy script. Sign in as the test user, turn on tools, create and share.

Figure 11: The four business-MCP connector cards, with the order-fulfillment agent added manually

Registry-sourced connectors are Custom MCP connectors (relevant for custom permissions). Removing the link later doesn’t delete connectors already created.

Figure 12: The Authenticate step using the authorization-code OAuth flow (OAUTH2_AUTHORIZATION_CODE)

Add the order-fulfillment agent connector

In the Amazon Quick web console: because it is an agent record, create its connector manually (Connectors → Create for your team → Model Context Protocol → Create new): name it sc-order-fulfillment-agent, point it at the AgentCore Runtime direct invocation URL from the deploy script, complete the same OAuth sign-in, create and share.

Figure 13: Creating the sc-order-fulfillment-agent connector, pointed at the AgentCore runtime invocation URL

Attach the connectors to your agent

The deployment creates the Supply Chain agent: a Quick Space, imported datasets and S3 knowledge base, and the agent with instructions, starter prompts, and welcome message. What remains is attaching the connectors.

In the Amazon Quick web console (agent settings): open the deployment-created Supply Chain agent (default id sc-supply-chain-agent) and attach all five connectors (four business MCPs plus sc-order-fulfillment-agent), or pass the five connector IDs to the setup script.

Set up proactive monitoring

To make it proactive, Quick runs the same agent on a schedule or on incoming email and posts results to the Activity Feed. Both paths reuse the agent and tools you configured.

In the Quick Desktop App (Settings → Connections): connect Outlook and turn on email monitoring. Then, in Quick Chat, create two natural-language schedules, time-based (“Every morning, check for new critical disruptions”) and email-driven (“Every two hours in business hours, check supplier replies and validate”). The agent extracts pricing, runs the checks, and posts a card.

Try it in Amazon Quick

With the agent and connectors ready, ask in natural language in Amazon Quick Chat. Each prompt shows the data-then-rules pattern.

Ask Amazon Quick What you get
“What supply chain tools do I have?” The five MCP connectors (quoting, governance, invoice, disruption alerts, order-fulfillment agent), with status.
“Show me active supply disruptions.” Active disruptions with severity, region, SKU counts (Disruption Alerts MCP).
“Assess the impact of the TechComp production halt.” Revenue at risk, affected orders, days of supply, from your datasets.
“Is this supplier an approved vendor, and do we have budget authority for a $72,000 PO?” An approval from the Governance MCP (vendor status, budget authority, compliance).
“Generate a contract-aligned quote for 1,000 units for this customer.” A contract-aligned quote from the Quoting MCP, as a branded document.
“A supplier just went down. Find alternatives, verify compliance, and issue an emergency RFQ.” The Order Fulfillment Agent chains disruption, governance, and quoting MCPs into one recommendation.

Conclusion

AgentCore and Amazon Quick are a repeatable enterprise-AI pattern: separate intelligence from interface. AgentCore turns fragmented backends into a composable, governed, AI-accessible layer through standard MCP interfaces. Amazon Quick democratizes access in natural language.

The gain is the collapsed decision chain: detect, research, decide, act, and log once spanned five tools, now one conversation. The AI researches, correlates, validates. The person decides. Every call is authenticated, authorized, policy-checked, and audited, and a 45-60 minute routine across five systems can collapse to minutes.

That is the shift from data-rich, insight-poor to data-rich, decision-ready. Start with one MCP server and one persona. The registry grows and the experience stays the same.

About the authors

Vineet Kachhawaha

Vineet is a Sr. Worldwide Agentic AI Solution Architect at AWS, focused on Amazon Quick. He works closely with enterprise customers and partners to design, deploy, and scale AI-driven solutions. Vineet also co-led the AWS for Legal Tech initiative, helping legal and compliance organizations harness AI/ML to drive business value. He loves building and tinkering with agentic AI solutions and considers himself a lifelong learner. Vineet regularly speaks at AWS events and industry conferences, sharing his expertise on generative AI and agentic architectures.

Kamlesh Mariwala

Kamlesh is a Senior Specialist Solutions Architect for Generative AI at Amazon Web Services (AWS), focused on the automotive and manufacturing industries. He helps customers design scalable, secure, and cost-effective architectures that use generative AI, agentic AI, and machine learning to solve complex business problems and speed up time to value.

Sachin Sathaye

Sachin is a Head of Data and AI GTM and Architectures at AWS, where he advises enterprise leaders on their data and AI transformations. He partners with CXOs to design, deploy, and scale AI-driven solutions that turn strategy into measurable business value, with focus on supply chain, commercial excellence, new product introduction, manufacturing operations, and enterprise business services. Sachin is the author of “The 12 Factors of Enterprise Agentic AI: A Value Chain,” a vendor-agnostic framework for building production-grade agentic systems, and a recognized voice on operationalizing generative and agentic AI at scale.

item.title: Fine-tuning GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
item.dc:creator: Mijanur Palash
item.description: Learn how we fine-tuned GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, and how to decide between supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning with GRPO. SFT took reasoning-language accuracy from 22% to 100%, and GRPO added measurable gains where headroom existed.
item.content:encoded:
GPT-OSS-20B is an open-weight reasoning model that thinks in English. Ask it to reason in French, German, Spanish, or Italian and it acknowledges the instruction, then produces its chain-of-thought in English anyway. On a 50-example multilingual reasoning test, the base model reasoned in the correct target language only 22 percent of the time. That 22 percent was almost entirely the English examples (English 100 percent, French 0 percent, German 10 percent, Spanish 0 percent, Italian 0 percent).

For teams deploying reasoning models for non-English users, that gap matters. A user who asks a question in French expects the model to reason and answer in French, not to switch to English mid-thought. Closing that gap is a fine-tuning problem. It raises a question every team faces once they start customizing open-weight models: supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), or both?

In this post, we walk through how we fine-tuned GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod. We show when SFT alone was sufficient and when GRPO added measurable value on top. To understand more broadly when GRPO helps, we also ran a controlled Qwen2.5-7B experiment across two tasks with different capability gaps. The short answer: SFT does most of the work, GRPO refines when there is headroom to refine, and matching the technique to the capability gap is what decides the outcome.

Solution overview

This section covers the multilingual reasoning task and dataset, how SFT and GRPO complement each other, and the training stack we ran on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod.

The task and dataset

The dataset is HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking — a chain-of-thought reasoning dataset translated into French, Spanish, German, and Italian alongside English, roughly 949 training and 50 validation examples. The model receives a reasoning language: system-prompt instruction and must both reason and answer in that target language, overriding its strong English prior. The evaluation is 50 test cases: 10 math/logic problems across 5 languages (EN/FR/DE/ES/IT).

Two metrics matter:

  • Reasoning-language correct – is the chain-of-thought in the requested language?
  • Answer-language correct – is the final answer in the requested language?

How SFT and GRPO fit together

The clearest way to think about the two techniques: SFT teaches a behavior the model doesn’t have. GRPO optimizes a behavior the model can already sometimes produce. GRPO works by sampling a group of responses per prompt and pushing the policy toward the above-average ones. If the desired behavior has zero probability in the base distribution, there is very little for GRPO to reinforce. That single idea explains almost every result in this post.

The training stack

We ran on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod with Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) orchestration. For the initial SFT and GRPO runs on GPT-OSS-20B, we used the PyTorch TRL library. For the Qwen control experiment, we switched to veRL as the trainer, with Ray and KubeRay for distributed orchestration and vLLM for fast rollout generation. Checkpoints and datasets lived on Amazon FSx for Lustre, and the inter-node fabric used Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA). All fine-tuning used Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), which is parameter-efficient and well-suited to both SFT and GRPO.

The following diagram shows the training data path end-to-end. A submission from the user lands on the Amazon EKS control plane of the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster. Amazon EKS schedules a Ray head pod plus worker pods that run the veRL trainer and vLLM rollout workers. Both sets of pods mount Amazon FSx for Lustre for the base model, training data, and checkpoints. Inter-node collectives use EFA. Rollouts stream from vLLM back to the veRL trainer, and the trainer writes checkpoints back to Amazon FSx for Lustre.

Figure 1: End-to-end training data path for SFT and GRPO fine-tuning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod with veRL, Ray, KubeRay, vLLM, and Amazon FSx for Lustre for Qwen control experiments

The following describes each hop in more detail. The submitter starts the run from Amazon SageMaker Studio or the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). The Amazon EKS control plane on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod places pods on GPU nodes and starts a Ray head with worker pods for the veRL trainer and the vLLM rollout workers. Amazon FSx for Lustre provides shared, high-throughput storage for the base model, the training data, and the checkpoints. When training completes, the trainer writes the LoRA adapter back to Amazon FSx for Lustre for downstream evaluation or serving.

Prerequisites

To follow along, you need:

  • An Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster with Amazon EKS orchestration. GPT-OSS SFT used 4× ml.g6e.12xlarge (16× L40S 48GB). The Qwen control used 2× g6e.48xlarge (16× L40S).
  • An Amazon FSx for Lustre file system mounted on the cluster with a PersistentVolumeClaim named fsx-claim at /fsx.
  • EFA-enabled instances and a working NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) and aws-ofi-nccl stack for multi-node SFT.
  • A container registry such as Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) to hold the training image built from the reference repository.
  • A HuggingFace access token for openai/gpt-oss-20b and the HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking dataset.
  • The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), kubectl, docker, and envsubst available on your workstation.

Set up the training environment

All of the commands, manifests, and scripts referenced below live in the awsome-distributed-ai GitHub repository under 3.test_cases/pytorch/trl/gpt-oss-lora-grpo/. Clone the repository and change into the test case directory:

git clone https://github.com/awslabs/awsome-distributed-ai
cd awsome-distributed-ai/3.test_cases/pytorch/trl/gpt-oss-lora-grpo

Copy the environment template, then edit env_vars to set your ECR registry, image name, tag, and HuggingFace token:

cp env_vars.example env_vars
source env_vars

Build the training image and push it to your registry. The image bundles PyTorch, TRL, HuggingFace Transformers, PEFT, and the training and inference scripts:

cd artifacts && ./build_push.sh && cd ..

Point kubectl at your cluster and apply the FSx storage manager pod. The storage manager gives you a shell into the shared file system for checkpoint conversion and eval-log inspection:

aws eks update-kubeconfig --name <YOUR_CLUSTER_NAME> --region us-east-2
envsubst '$REGISTRY $IMAGE $TAG $HF_TOKEN' \
  < kubernetes/fsx-storage-manager.yaml | kubectl apply -f -

Fine-tune GPT-OSS-20B with SFT and LoRA

We begin by measuring the base model, then configure the SFT run and examine the results.

The base-model gap

Base GPT-OSS-20B on the 50-case eval scored 22 percent reasoning-language correct (11/50). Per-language: English 100 percent, French 0 percent, German 10 percent, Spanish 0 percent, Italian 0 percent. The model defaults to English reasoning regardless of the instruction.

SFT configuration

The SFT setup used LoRA r=8, α=16, trained for 1,000 steps on 4× ml.g6e.12xlarge (16× L40S 48GB) with Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) full-shard, bf16 precision, and gradient checkpointing. The job runs as an elastic HyperPodPyTorchJob managed by Kueue, launched with hyperpodrun.

Apply the SFT manifest:

envsubst '$REGISTRY $IMAGE $TAG $HF_TOKEN' \
  < hyperpod-eks/train-lora-hyperpod-elastic-g6e.yaml | kubectl apply -f -

Watch training progress:

kubectl get pods -l app=gpt-oss-lora-elastic
kubectl logs -f -l app=gpt-oss-lora-elastic

Loss and gradient norm print each step. A healthy run looks like this:

{'loss': 1.035, 'grad_norm': 0.163, 'learning_rate': 0.0002, 'mean_token_accuracy': 0.716, 'epoch': 3.25}
{'loss': 1.003, 'grad_norm': 0.171, 'lr': 0.0002, 'acc': 0.722, 'epoch': 3.32}
{'loss': 0.976, 'grad_norm': 0.159, 'lr': 0.0002, 'acc': 0.726, 'epoch': 3.57}

When training completes, convert the FSDP checkpoint to the Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) format that TRL’s GRPO trainer and the inference scripts expect:

kubectl exec -it fsx-storage-manager -- python /app/convert_fsdp_checkpoint.py \
  --checkpoint /fsx/checkpoints/checkpoint-1000 \
  --output    /fsx/checkpoints/converted-peft/lora-checkpoint-1000-peft

SFT results and the staged learning curve

After SFT, the model reasons in the correct language 100 percent of the time (50/50) across all five languages. SFT learned this in two stages:

  • Around step 200, the model learned to reason in the target language (reasoning-language metric hits 100 percent).
  • Around step 1000, the model additionally learned to give the answer in the target language.

Final SFT eval (step 1000):

  • Reasoning-language correct: 100 percent (50/50).
  • Answer-language correct: 62 percent (31/50).
  • Both correct: 62 percent (31/50).
  • Per-language answer accuracy: FR 60 percent, DE 60 percent, ES 30 percent, IT 60 percent, EN 100 percent.

Takeaway: SFT is not optional here. The base model can’t follow the reasoning-language instruction at all, and SFT takes reasoning-language from 22 percent to 100 percent. The remaining gap is answer-language at 62 percent. That’s the harder half, because the final answer is short and the English prior is strongest there.

Refine answer-language with GRPO

Answer-language was the obvious target for GRPO. SFT already produced correct reasoning 100 percent of the time, and the model sometimes produced the answer in the right language, so there was a signal to reinforce.

Run GRPO on top of the SFT checkpoint

We ran GRPO with TRL’s GRPOTrainer, starting from the SFT checkpoint. The setup: load the SFT LoRA, call merge_and_unload, and add a new LoRA (r=8, α=16, about 0.068 percent trainable parameters, 13.6M of 20B). Training used K=8 generations per prompt, device_map=auto, learning rate 1e-6, and 10 epochs. The reward function scored answer-language (±5.0), reasoning-language (±1.5), and brevity (+0.5 or −1.0), for a combined range of −7.5 to +7.0.

Launch GRPO from the converted SFT checkpoint:

envsubst '$REGISTRY $IMAGE $TAG $HF_TOKEN' \
  < kubernetes/train-grpo-singlenode.yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl logs -f grpo-single

GRPO writes checkpoints to /fsx/checkpoints/grpo-singlenode/. Pick the best checkpoint against your held-out eval (the answer-language metric peaked early in this run) and convert it to PEFT format for inference and evaluation.

Result (from the SFT checkpoint):

  • Reasoning-language correct: 100 percent (held: GRPO didn’t break what SFT taught).
  • Answer-language correct: 62 to 70 percent (+8 points, 35/50).
  • Both correct: 70 percent.
  • Per-language answer: FR 70 percent, DE 80 percent, ES 60 percent, IT 40 percent, EN 100 percent.

GRPO delivered a real +8 point gain on the answer-language metric while holding reasoning at 100 percent. The gain came where there was headroom to gain. Answer-language was the sometimes-correct behavior that SFT had not fully converged on, and GRPO reinforced it.

Compare base, SFT, and GRPO inference side by side

To see the qualitative difference, deploy three inference pods that share the same base model but load different adapters:

envsubst '$REGISTRY $IMAGE $TAG $HF_TOKEN' \
  < kubernetes/inference-g6e-base.yaml    | kubectl apply -f -
envsubst '$REGISTRY $IMAGE $TAG $HF_TOKEN' \
  < kubernetes/inference-g6e-trained.yaml | kubectl apply -f -
envsubst '$REGISTRY $IMAGE $TAG $HF_TOKEN' \
  < kubernetes/inference-g6e-grpo.yaml    | kubectl apply -f -

Run the same French-reasoning prompt through each variant:

kubectl exec -it inference-base    -- python /app/inference_g6e.py \
  --reasoning_language French

kubectl exec -it inference-trained -- python /app/inference_g6e.py \
  --checkpoint /fsx/checkpoints/converted-peft/lora-checkpoint-1000-peft \
  --reasoning_language French

kubectl exec -it inference-grpo    -- python /app/inference_grpo_new.py \
  --use_grpo \
  --grpo_checkpoint /fsx/checkpoints/converted-peft/checkpoint-1470-peft \
  --reasoning_language French

The base pod reasons in English despite the instruction. The SFT pod reasons in French but often answers in English. The GRPO pod reasons and answers in French. To reproduce the full 50-case eval that generated the numbers earlier, run the evaluation manifest and read the result file from the FSx storage manager:

envsubst '$REGISTRY $IMAGE $TAG $HF_TOKEN' \
  < kubernetes/eval-grpo.yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl logs -f eval-grpo
kubectl exec fsx-storage-manager -- \
  cat /fsx/experiments/grpo_eval_checkpoint1470_*.txt

To understand more broadly when GRPO adds value, we ran a controlled experiment on Qwen2.5-7B across two tasks with different capability gaps.

Test the pattern with a Qwen2.5-7B control

To test the “match technique to capability gap” thesis on a different model and different tasks, we ran controlled experiments on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. The first task is the same multilingual reasoning task (where headroom exists). The second task is GSM8K, where the model is already at peak accuracy. This is an internal experiment, and the public repo has not yet been released.

Infrastructure: 2× g6e.48xlarge (16× L40S), EFA 100Gbps, FSx Lustre, Ray 2.44 + KubeRay 1.4.2, veRL v0.6.1, vLLM 0.8.4.

Arms: A = base, B = SFT-only, C = SFT+GRPO.

Multilingual reasoning (50 cases)

Metric A base B SFT C SFT+GRPO Δ GRPO
Structured format 0% 92% 98% +6
Reasoning language 0% 96% 98% +2
Answer language 0% 38% 44% +6
Both correct 0% 38% 44% +6

GSM8K, a task with no headroom

On GSM8K, base Qwen2.5-7B already scores 90.5 percent (181/200). GRPO at step 30 also scores 90.5 percent. When most sampled groups are all-correct, the group-relative advantage collapses to zero, so there is no learning signal. This is the other half of the thesis: GRPO needs headroom (pass@k >> pass@1) to have anything to optimize. No headroom means no gain.

Best practices

  1. Start with SFT. GRPO cannot teach a behavior with zero base probability. It can only reinforce responses the model already sometimes produces. SFT took reasoning-language from 22 percent to 100 percent, and every GRPO win in this work was built on that SFT checkpoint.
  2. Use LoRA for both SFT and GRPO. LoRA r=8/α=16 was parameter-efficient (0.068 percent trainable), and on the Qwen control it stayed numerically stable through GRPO (grad norm 0.23, about 11.7 GB per GPU). It’s a strong default when you want SFT and GRPO to share the same adapter shape.
  3. Match the technique to the gap. Use SFT for missing behavior. Use GRPO for refining an existing, sometimes-correct behavior. GRPO’s realistic ceiling here was +6 to +8 points.
  4. Check for reward headroom before spending GPU-hours. If most groups are all-correct (GSM8K 90.5 percent base), the group-relative advantage collapses to zero and GRPO gets no gradient. Verify there is headroom (pass@k >> pass@1) before starting a GRPO run.

Clean up resources

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the workload resources and then the underlying infrastructure:

  1. Delete the training and inference pods and jobs: 
    kubectl delete hyperpodpytorchjob lora-hyperpod-elastic --ignore-not-found
kubectl delete pod grpo-single inference-base inference-trained inference-grpo \
  eval-grpo fsx-storage-manager --ignore-not-found
  2. Scale down or delete the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster or its node groups.
  3. Delete the Amazon FSx for Lustre file system once you have exported any checkpoints you want to keep.
  4. Delete any Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) buckets or objects used for training data or checkpoint archives.

Conclusion

We showed how to fine-tune GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, and how to decide between SFT and GRPO. SFT did most of the work: reasoning-language went from 22 percent to 100 percent. GRPO added a real, modest refinement on top (answer 62 percent to 70 percent) where headroom existed. A parallel Qwen2.5-7B control confirmed the pattern. GRPO added +6 percent on multilingual reasoning, where there was room to improve. It added no gain on GSM8K, where the model was already at peak accuracy (90.5 percent).

Decision framework:

  • Behavior the model can’t do at all: use SFT.
  • Behavior it does sometimes, with headroom: use SFT then GRPO for a few points more.
  • Model already at peak accuracy, or target has zero base probability: GRPO won’t help.

To try this yourself, walk through the test cases in the awsome-distributed-ai repository. For more on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, see the service detail page and the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod documentation. For a walkthrough of Ray on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, see the related post Running distributed training on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod with Ray and Amazon SageMaker Studio. The link will be added after that post is published. Share your results in the comments.

 

About the authors

Mijanur Palash

Mijanur is a Specialist Solutions Architect on the AI/ML Infrastructure team at AWS. He focuses on distributed training and reinforcement learning workloads on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod for automotive, pharmaceutical, and generative AI customers. Outside of work, Palash enjoys hiking and photography.

Mark Vinciguerra

Mark was a Worldwide Specialist Solutions Architect for Generative AI at AWS, focused on distributed training and inference on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod. He works with strategic customers on large-scale foundation-model workloads across EKS and Slurm orchestration and contributes reference architectures and workshops for HyperPod, Ray, and SageMaker Unified Studio.

item.title: How Octave built a secure multi-tenant AI foundation on Amazon Bedrock
item.dc:creator: Urvish Saraiya
item.description: Octave built a secure, multi-tenant AI foundation on Amazon Bedrock, using Cohere Embed v4 for embeddings and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for isolated agent execution, to power a Complaint Triage Assistant that searches 2 billion regulated documents without crossing tenant boundaries.
item.content:encoded:
In quality management for regulated industries, the institutional memory that resolves a problem is almost always buried somewhere in a customer’s history. A similar defect investigated last year, a Corrective and Preventive Action (CAPA) that fixed the root cause, an audit finding that flagged the same gap. That knowledge sits in billions of documents no human can search by semantic similarity across languages and formats, so every investigation starts from scratch. Octave Reliance has helped each organization collect documents across multiple systems to help them search more easily and keep track of everything they have. The Octave Reliance team saw unlocking this history as its single largest opportunity to help customers work faster and stay compliant. The obstacle was equally clear: complaint records, audit findings, and corrective actions carry the platform’s strictest isolation requirements, and those were exactly the records the AI would need to read. In a platform serving over 14,000 customers across medical devices, pharmaceuticals, and food manufacturing, a single inadvertent disclosure from one customer to another would carry regulatory consequences far outweighing any AI benefit.

Octave operates across 180 countries, serving more than 60% of the Global Fortune 500. Its cloud-native quality management system, Reliance, supports over 650 enterprise customers with over 40 applications, from complaint management and CAPA tracking to audit management and supplier quality. Everyone generates regulated data that AI could reason over. Each customer is a separate tenant and no data can cross a tenant boundary.

Faced with that, the Reliance team made an unusual call: rather than shipping one AI feature, it spent its first cycle building a foundation every future feature would sit on. That foundation has since cut deployment time per use case by 50 percent. If you are bringing AI to a software as a service (SaaS) platform where the data is valuable, but isolation is non-negotiable, the reasoning travels beyond quality management. In this post, we walk through the four tensions that shaped the design and the three-layer foundation Octave built with Cohere Embed v4 on Amazon Bedrock. We then follow the pipeline that embedded 2 billion documents and the Complaint Triage Assistant that proved it in production.

Why a foundation, not a feature

Envisioning workshops with AWS surfaced four high-impact use cases: complaint summarization and triage, audit readiness monitoring, incident narrative generation, and predictive quality risk scoring. They also surfaced the insight that shaped everything after dozens of applications, each with different document types and workflows. Building AI for one in a silo meant rebuilding the infrastructure for the next.

So, the team inverted the plan: build the horizontal platform first, then cut vertical feature slices into it. Complaint summarization and triage went first, to prove the architecture before the rest followed.

The four tensions

Before selecting a single model, the team spent its time on four problems that pulled in different directions. None could be traded away.

Making data available without risking inadvertent disclosure. Complaint records, CAPAs, standard operating procedures (SOPs), and audit findings belong to one tenant and must be unreachable by another. Not even an errant AI query could cross. Vector store, retrieval logic, and generation context all had to be scoped to a single tenant.

Executing agents in isolation. The permissions governing an agent’s tools, data stores, and model endpoints had to be scoped to the requesting user rather than a shared service role, available only during execution, and respectful of that user’s access rights. A shared agent pool with static credentials failed all three.

Reading content that cannot be trusted. Agents here ingest complaints, email attachments, scanned PDFs, and images from outside the organization. The OWASP Top 10 for large language model (LLM) Applications (2025) names the threats that apply directly: prompt injection through ingested content (LLM01), sensitive information disclosure (LLM02), improper output handling (LLM05), and excessive agency (LLM06). Hidden instructions in an attached PDF are not hypothetical at this volume.

Embedding 2 billion documents without a quarter-long wait. Reliance hosts more than 2 billion documents, with individual tenants storing millions of Word files, PDFs, scanned forms, spreadsheets, images, and email. The team committed to onboarding even the largest tenant within a single working day. Because these documents inform regulatory decisions, quality could not be traded for throughput. A missed complaint erodes trust in the whole system.

Where the architecture landed

Holding four tensions at once narrowed the options considerably. Amazon Bedrock addressed them as one platform: multi-model access through a single API, the AWS Region residency and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) governance the AWS account already enforces, and Guardrails as production content controls rather than something to build.

The foundation resolves into three layers, shown in Figure 1. Data preparation embeds quality documents with Cohere Embed v4 on Amazon Bedrock and writes them to a per-tenant vector store on Amazon OpenSearch Service. Secure execution passes a user request through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which applies authentication and policy before handing it to an isolated microVM session that calls an Anthropic Claude model on Amazon Bedrock. Wrapping both, content protection applies Amazon Bedrock Guardrails twice: input filtering on the way in, output filtering before anything reaches the handler. Retrieval, execution, and screening stay in separate stages, so each can be enforced and evidenced on its own.

Figure 1: High-level architecture of the Reliance AI foundation

Choosing how to represent the data

Nothing else worked until the documents were retrievable. That meant accurately, across languages and formats, and not across a tenant boundary. The team evaluated embedding models against its own corpus rather than public leaderboards. The deciding questions were specific to this data: what a photo of a cracked housing has to do with the paragraph describing it, and a German complaint with an English CAPA.

Cohere Embed v4 on Amazon Bedrock won on five counts and they weren’t independent of each other. What was decided first was how much of the pipeline was made unnecessary. Quality records carry photos of defective products, scanned inspection forms, and annotated diagrams alongside text. Embed v4 places both modalities in one vector space. A photo of a cracked housing and the paragraph describing that defect are retrievable from a single query, with no separate pipeline per modality. Native multilingual support does the same work along the other axis: documents arrive in multiple languages, often inside one tenant’s corpus, and need no translation preprocessing. Two pipelines the team never had to build, and two fewer places for a document to fall out of retrieval.

The remaining three counts settled where the vectors could live and what they would cost. Customer data can’t leave its AWS Region, even for inference, so in-Region model availability on Amazon Bedrock was a precondition rather than a convenience. Embed v4 supports in-Region inference in the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1), Europe (Ireland) Region (eu-west-1), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo) Region (ap-northeast-1), covering three of Octave’s regional compliance requirements. Model and feature availability varies by Region and changes over time. For current coverage, see Regional availability by models in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. Within each Region, Amazon OpenSearch Service costs scale linearly with dimension count. That made Embed v4’s configurable output dimensions of 256–1,536 worth testing rather than accepting by default. Testing against representative production queries showed 512 dimensions holding target accuracy while cutting storage roughly 66 percent against the 1,536 default. The 128K token context window paid off elsewhere entirely: chunks of roughly 4K tokens pack many to a request, which is where the onboarding throughput came from.

Keeping tenants apart at runtime

The harder question was where to enforce tenant separation. Application code would have worked, but it would have meant every future feature team getting it right on every code path, where one missed check risks inadvertent cross-tenant disclosure. The team pushed isolation into the runtime instead. AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, enforces separation below the application layer, and because it stays framework- and model-independent, the agent framework and models chosen for the Complaint Triage Assistant were not constrained by the isolation decision.

Each user session runs in a dedicated microVM with its own CPU, memory, and filesystem, stopped and sanitized when the session ends. That is hardware-level separation designed to hold regardless of how the agent behaves. AgentCore carries the authenticated user’s identity through the whole execution chain: per-user OAuth token vaults verify the agent acts for that specific user rather than a shared service identity, and credentials are scoped per-agent and live only during the session. AgentCore Gateway authorizes at the tool, operation, and parameter level. Automated reasoning provides formal verification against the defined rules. It’s the same discipline behind IAM and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) policy validation. Figure 2 traces that separation across two tenants.

Figure 2: AgentCore session separation between tenants. Each microVM is stopped after use with memory sanitized.

A complaint submitted by a quality handler at Tenant A therefore reaches only Tenant A’s token vault, tools, and sandbox in AgentCore Code Interpreter, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Tenant B’s session has no path to any of them.

Treating ingested content as untrusted

This tension had no clean answer. A complaint attachment is untrusted input, but it’s also the thing the agent exists to read, so suspicious content couldn’t be rejected. The team settled on defense in depth.

Octave applied Amazon Bedrock Guardrails over the agent logic rather than inside it, at three points in the complaint workflow. The ApplyGuardrail API evaluates text extracted from attachments before embedding, retrieved documents and tool outputs before they enter the agent’s context, and the synthesized brief before the handler sees it. Attachment-derived content is passed with input tagging, marking it as data rather than instruction. That is what makes an injection buried mid-document detectable. Personally Identifiable Information (PII) is masked on the way in.

Detection alone wasn’t sufficient, so bounded agency sits underneath. Whatever an agent is asked to do, AgentCore Gateway still governs which tools it can invoke, and document extraction runs in the AgentCore Code Interpreter sandbox with no network egress and no persistence beyond the session. A payload hidden in a PDF has to defeat every layer, not one.

The effect: detection and masking rates are tracked per tenant, so what the screening caught is something Octave can evidence rather than assert.

Getting 2 billion documents through the pipeline

Ahead of the embedding model sat the harder problem: extracting usable content from Word files, spreadsheets, digital PDFs, scanned pages, photographs, and email threads. Several languages appear, sometimes inside one record. And it had to run fast enough that onboarding took a day rather than a quarter. Figure 3 traces the resulting pipeline end to end.

Figure 3: Ingestion pipeline: event-driven document processing from the application platform through Step Functions orchestration to the per-tenant OpenSearch index.

Document events fan out through Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) and Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) into an AWS Step Functions state machine. That state machine orchestrates parsing, chunking, and embedding across concurrent AWS Lambda executions inside a dedicated Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC). Because parallelism comes from fanning batches across executions rather than scaling one resource, throughput grows without rearchitecting.

Parsing handles the heterogeneity: semantic hierarchy preserved from Word files and spreadsheets, optical character recognition (OCR) applied to scanned PDFs lacking a text layer, embedded images treated as first-class content. Chunks carry metadata: tenant, document type, source application, language, and a content hash. That metadata drives both retrieval filtering and per-tenant namespace enforcement.

The throughput came from packing. Interleaving many 4K chunks into single requests against Embed v4’s 128K context window cut the API calls for a large corpus by about an order of magnitude. In Octave’s internal testing on Amazon Bedrock, Embed v4 delivered 28 million tokens per minute. After tuning batch sizes with Cohere’s solutions architects until memory bottlenecks cleared, the pipeline sustained 1.4 million documents per 24 hours per tenant workload. That is what made the single-working-day commitment real.

The Complaint Triage Assistant

A hospital reports defective syringes to a medical device manufacturer, and the record lands with email, photos of damaged units, and supporting documentation attached. A quality handler has to piece the context together across those formats, work out whether anything like it has been reported before, and find what resolved it. Only then can a priority be assigned, often inside a reporting window measured in days.

The assistant is built with the Strands Agents SDK, open-sourced by AWS, which composes agentic workflows as graphs, with nodes as tool invocations or model calls and edges as the data dependencies between them. AgentCore runtime runs that graph and isolates it per session, and five stages carry a complaint from raw attachments to a finished brief.

Document extraction comes first. PDFs, images, email attachments, and videos all enter AgentCore Code Interpreter, which parses each artifact into a structured intermediate representation. A Claude model on Amazon Bedrock then summarizes the record, and that summary, rather than the raw multi-thousand-token source, becomes the retrieval query. Retrieval runs it against the tenant’s OpenSearch index of Embed v4 embeddings, surfacing similar past complaints and their CAPAs, with AgentCore Gateway enforcing that only authorized namespaces are reachable.

What comes back is not trusted on similarity alone. A separate model call scores results by confidence and discards matches that share vocabulary but differ in root cause. What survives goes to synthesis, where Anthropic Claude Sonnet on Amazon Bedrock assembles the output: key facts, sentiment, urgency indicators, the closest historical records with their outcomes, and a recommended triage priority.

Completed briefs are cached in Amazon DynamoDB with a per-environment time to live (TTL), so repeated views cost nothing extra. The handler no longer starts from zero, but from institutional memory.

Figure 4 places that engine behind a private API boundary. A portal request reaches AgentCore runtime through a private Amazon API Gateway and a Lambda function, and retrieval reads the document index through role-based access with pre-signed URLs while attachments stay in Amazon S3. Cached summaries and OpenTelemetry traces exit to the summarization table and the evaluation dashboard.

Figure 4: Summarizing engine: the AgentCore-powered workflow handling document extraction, retrieval, reasoning, and synthesis within a private API boundary, with response caching and full observability.

Figure 5 reduces the same path to a single line, with Guardrails filtering at both ends.

Figure 5: Complaint Triage Assistant pipeline from ingestion to handler output

Proving what the agent did

Observability here is not only how the engineering team debugs but also how they integrate with system auditing capabilities to meet compliance requirements. An auditor can ask why a particular complaint was triaged the way it was, and “the model decided” will not survive that conversation.

AgentCore captures OpenTelemetry-compatible traces across every node of the graph: each model call, retrieval, and AgentCore Code Interpreter run. Months later, Octave can show which retrieved documents and prompts produced a given brief. The model invocation logging of Amazon Bedrock adds a per-tenant record of every request and response, scoped through the IAM identity AgentCore propagates, with costs attributing to the initiating tenant in Amazon CloudWatch.

Offline, AgentCore Evals reruns the workflow against expert-annotated ground truth after any change to prompts, models, or retrieval parameters, reporting summarization faithfulness, retrieval precision at K, and output completeness. A prompt that reads better but retrieves worse gets caught before users see it.

Results

The Complaint Triage Assistant has been running in production for three months, and the following numbers reflect that period.

The handler who used to open an investigation with nothing now opens it with the relevant history already assembled. The 4–6 hours Octave measures per investigation is the work the pipeline absorbed: extraction across formats, the hunt for precedent, and the reading it takes to tell a genuinely similar defect from a coincidence of wording.

The foundation also changed how quickly Octave ships. By its own accounting, development cycles for new AI capabilities went from months to weeks. Shared data preparation, secure execution, and retrieval are the three layers of Figure 1. They cut deployment time per use case by 50 percent, because each new capability inherits them rather than rebuilding them. That landed semantic search in Q2, two quarters ahead of the original Q4 target.

Looking back

The decision to build a foundation first was the one the team second-guessed most. Months of infrastructure work is hard to defend when stakeholders want an AI feature they can see. The next round of use cases has borne it out. Two choices carried it: isolation pushed into microVM sessions and identity propagation rather than application code, and embedding models evaluated against Octave’s own corpus, which surfaced the 512-dimension trade-off no benchmark would have shown.

The team also drew a line it chose not to cross. The assistant surfaces context and precedent. The quality handler still makes the call. In an industry where that call carries regulatory weight, that boundary shaped what got automated and what did not.

What’s next

Octave is now extending the foundation across the Reliance suite. Audit readiness monitoring, incident narrative generation, and predictive quality risk scoring are next, each building on the same infrastructure.

If your platform faces a similar tension: valuable data behind hard isolation requirements. Octave’s experience shows the trade-offs are workable. To learn more about the services behind this story, see Amazon Bedrock, the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation, and Cohere on Amazon Bedrock. For related architectural guidance, see AWS vector solutions: Build agentic AI where your data lives and Scaling agentic AI: Enterprise patterns without vendor lock-in.

About the authors

Urvish Saraiya

Urvish is an engineering leader at Octave, where he is building an industrial AI platform on AWS. With over 18 years of experience in distributed software systems, data platforms, and machine learning, he brings deep technical expertise across public safety, payments, and digital marketing. Urvish combines strong technical skills with a strategic, product minded approach, focused on solving business needs with commercial impact.

Manu is a Senior Solutions Architect at AWS with over 18 years of experience in the software industry, specializing in artificial intelligence, data and analytics, and security. His expertise spans strategic oversight and hands-on technical leadership, where he reviews and guides the work of both internal and external customers. You can connect with or follow Manu on LinkedIn.

Madhunika Reddy Mikkili

Madhunika is a Data and Machine Learning Engineer at AWS. She helps enterprise customers solve complex business problems with Generative AI and Machine Learning.

Payal is a Solutions Architect at Cohere with over 15 years of cross-domain expertise in DevOps, Cloud, Security, SDN, Data Center Architecture, and Virtualization. She drives partnerships at Cohere and helps customers with complex GenAI solution integrations.

Nate is a Senior Partner Development Manager who helps leading generative AI model providers grow their revenue through AWS partnership. Nate has been with Amazon Web Services for nearly 10 years. Nate is located in Seattle, WA, and enjoys outdoor activities and learning about emerging technologies. You can connect with or follow Nate on LinkedIn.

item.title: Access OpenAI GPT models on Amazon Bedrock from Canada with cross-Region inference
item.dc:creator: Roopesh Ramklass
item.description: Canadian organizations can now access OpenAI GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 models on Amazon Bedrock from the Canada (Central) and Canada West (Calgary) Regions using cross-Region inference. This post covers the models and inference profiles, how to set up permissions, and how to invoke them with the Responses, Chat Completions, and Converse APIs.
item.content:encoded:
Canadian organizations building generative AI applications on Amazon Bedrock often need the latest foundation models (FMs), such as OpenAI GPT-6.1, OpenAI GPT-6, and GPT-5.6, accessible from the Canadian AWS Regions. With Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference (CRIS), you can now access these models from Canada. OpenAI GPT-5.6 models (Sol, Terra, and Luna), GPT-6 (Astra, Sol, and Luna), and GPT-6.1 Sol are available from the Canada (Central) and Canada West (Calgary) Regions. Inference is processed in North America, with data-residency controls described later in this post.

Cross-Region inference is a capacity mechanism. Your application calls the Amazon Bedrock Runtime endpoint in your source Region. Amazon Bedrock then routes the request to a supported destination Region for processing. With this approach, you get access to a broader capacity pool that can help your application sustain throughput during demand spikes. You don’t need to manage destination Region routing in your application.

In this post, we walk through the GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 models available from Canada and the cross-Region inference profiles that serve them. We then show how to set up permissions and invoke the models with the OpenAI Responses API, Chat Completions API, and the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. For the Responses API, we include streaming and tool-use examples. Finally, we cover how to request quota increases, review the observability signals available in your source Region, and clean up when you are done.

Models available from Canada

With Amazon Bedrock, you can access three families of OpenAI models in Canada through cross-Region inference. The following table summarizes each model and its positioning.

Model Positioning
GPT-6.1 Sol Strong reasoning and coding for tasks where both performance and cost matter
GPT-6 Astra Complex end-to-end reasoning and agentic tasks
GPT-6 Sol Strong reasoning and coding for recurring tasks with economics suited to regular use
GPT-6 Luna Fast, low-cost inference for high-volume repeated tasks with adjustable reasoning effort per request
GPT-5.6 Sol High reasoning, coding, and agentic workloads
GPT-5.6 Terra Balanced performance and cost for everyday production
GPT-5.6 Luna Fast and affordable for high-volume, latency-sensitive applications

These models accept text and image inputs, return text, and support a 1-million-token context window, reasoning mode, and tool calling. GPT-6.1 Sol supports the same context window and tool calling, with additional input and output modalities documented in its model card. GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 also support prompt caching on Amazon Bedrock (see the Prompt caching section). These models are available through the OpenAI Responses API, the OpenAI Chat Completions API, and the Amazon Bedrock Converse API on the bedrock-runtime endpoint.

For pricing, see Amazon Bedrock pricing. For per-model Region availability, see the model cards in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide.

Cross-Region inference profiles from Canada

Amazon Bedrock inference profiles are logical identifiers you pass in place of a raw model ID. Each profile defines a model and the set of Regions to which Amazon Bedrock can route a request. Two profile types are available from Canada:

  • US geographic (prefixed us.) routes requests to your Canadian source Region and US Regions. Choose this profile when your workload requires inference processing to remain within North America (Canada and the US).
  • Global (prefixed global.) routes requests to supported commercial AWS Regions where the model is deployed. This draws on a broader capacity pool at the time of the request.

Endpoint availability differs by model and source Region, as shown in the following table.

Model US geographic profile Global profile
GPT-6.1 Sol ca-central-1, ca-west-1 ca-central-1, ca-west-1
GPT-6 Astra / Sol / Luna ca-central-1, ca-west-1 ca-central-1, ca-west-1
GPT-5.6 Sol / Terra / Luna ca-central-1, ca-west-1 ca-central-1

Profile membership and model availability can change. The global profile for the GPT-5.6 models is available only from ca-central-1. From ca-west-1, use the US geographic profile for GPT-5.6. Verify the active profiles for your source Region before deployment, either with the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) or on the console (see the following section), or see the Cross-Region inference support documentation.

Getting started

The following sections walk through the setup and code needed to invoke these models from your Canadian source Region.

Prerequisites

Before you begin, confirm that you have the following:

  • An AWS account with the Canada (Central) ca-central-1 or Canada West (Calgary) ca-west-1 Region enabled as your source Region.
  • An AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role or user with permissions to invoke the inference profiles (see Set up permissions).
  • A service control policy (SCP) that allows the inference profiles in your source Region, if your organization enforces SCPs (see SCP considerations).
  • Python 3.9 or later with the openai, boto3, and aws-bedrock-token-generator packages installed.

Set up permissions

For quick exploration, attach the AWS managed policy AmazonBedrockLimitedAccess. For deployed workloads with stricter access controls, use a least-privilege custom policy. The following example grants access to the GPT-6 Astra global profile from ca-central-1:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["bedrock:InvokeModel*"],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:bedrock:ca-central-1::inference-profile/global.openai.gpt-6-astra"
      ]
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["bedrock:InvokeModel*"],
      "Resource": ["arn:aws:bedrock:*::foundation-model/openai.gpt-6-astra"],
      "Condition": {
        "StringLike": {
          "bedrock:InferenceProfileArn": "arn:aws:bedrock:ca-central-1::inference-profile/global.openai.gpt-6-astra"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

If you authenticate through the API-key path (bearer token for the OpenAI SDK), also grant bedrock:CallWithBearerToken. For the Responses API, add bedrock:InvokeModel on arn:aws:bedrock:ca-central-1:*:project/default.

SCP considerations

If your organization restricts Regions through SCPs, use the bedrock:InferenceProfileArn condition key to allow CRIS traffic while blocking direct calls to unapproved Regions. The following SCP denies Amazon Bedrock inference outside your approved source Regions unless the request uses a CRIS inference profile:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyBedrockOutsideCanadaUnlessCris",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": ["bedrock:InvokeModel*"],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotEquals": {
          "aws:RequestedRegion": ["ca-central-1", "ca-west-1"]
        },
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "bedrock:InferenceProfileArn": [
            "arn:aws:bedrock:*:*:inference-profile/us.openai.*",
            "arn:aws:bedrock:*:*:inference-profile/global.openai.*"
          ]
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

With this condition, Amazon Bedrock can route to the profile’s destination Regions even when those Regions are otherwise denied by your SCP. Every destination Region in your chosen profile must be allowed for the request to succeed. For more detail, see Set up cross-Region inference in multi-account environments.

Verify active inference profiles

Before invoking a model, you can verify which profiles are active in your source Region with the AWS CLI. The following command lists the active OpenAI profiles from ca-central-1. To run the same check from Calgary, replace ca-central-1 with ca-west-1.

aws bedrock list-inference-profiles \
    --region ca-central-1 \
    --type-equals SYSTEM_DEFINED \
    --query "inferenceProfileSummaries[?contains(inferenceProfileId, 'openai')].[inferenceProfileId,status]" \
    --output table

The Amazon Bedrock console offers the same view. Open the console, choose Canada (Central) or Canada West (Calgary) as your Region, choose Cross-Region inference under Inference, and review the available profiles.

The following screenshot shows the active OpenAI inference profiles listed on the Amazon Bedrock console for the Canada (Central) Region.

Figure 1: Active OpenAI cross-Region inference profiles on the Amazon Bedrock console (Canada (Central))

Invoke the models through Amazon Bedrock Runtime

GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 support three access paths on the bedrock-runtime endpoint: the OpenAI Responses API, the OpenAI Chat Completions API, and the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. The OpenAI-compatible APIs are called on the /openai/v1 paths of the endpoint. The endpoint accepts either AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) or an Amazon Bedrock API key.

The following examples use the Amazon Bedrock token generator for Python to create a short-term Amazon Bedrock API key from your current AWS credentials, so your application does not need to store a static key.

OpenAI Responses API

For applications that already use the OpenAI SDK with the Responses API, point the client at the Regional Amazon Bedrock Runtime endpoint and pass the inference profile ID as the model.

from aws_bedrock_token_generator import provide_token
from openai import OpenAI

region = "ca-central-1"  # Use "ca-west-1" for Calgary
client = OpenAI(
    base_url=f"https://bedrock-runtime.{region}.amazonaws.com/openai/v1",
    api_key=provide_token(region=region),
)

response = client.responses.create(
    model="global.openai.gpt-6-astra",
    input="What are the key considerations for AI governance in Canadian financial services?",
    max_output_tokens=1024,
)
print(response.output_text)

For streaming output, set stream=True and iterate over the response events, printing text as it arrives:

stream = client.responses.create(
    model="global.openai.gpt-6-luna",
    input="List five generative AI use cases for Canadian healthcare.",
    max_output_tokens=512,
    stream=True,
)
for event in stream:
    if event.type == "response.output_text.delta":
        print(event.delta, end="", flush=True)

OpenAI Chat Completions API

The OpenAI Chat Completions format works through the same endpoint.

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="global.openai.gpt-5.6-terra",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize recent AI regulatory trends in Canada."}],
    max_completion_tokens=1024,
    reasoning_effort="low",
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)

For the full list of supported parameters, including reasoning effort levels, see the model cards in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide.

Amazon Bedrock Converse API

Use the Converse API when your application calls Amazon Bedrock through an AWS SDK. Boto3 resolves credentials through the standard AWS credential chain.

import boto3

bedrock = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="ca-central-1")
response = bedrock.converse(
    modelId="us.openai.gpt-5.6-terra",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Summarize recent AI regulatory trends in Canada."}]}],
    inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 1024},
)
# GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 may return a reasoningContent block alongside the text.
# Select the block that contains the text output.
text_output = next(block["text"] for block in response["output"]["message"]["content"] if "text" in block)
print(text_output)

The same call works for GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, and GPT-6.1 Sol by changing the inference profile ID. The following example uses the US geographic profile for GPT-6 Sol and the global profile for GPT-6 Luna. Both were validated from ca-central-1.

# GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, and GPT-6.1 Sol are called the same way. Swap the inference profile ID, and choose a us. (US geographic) or global. profile to match your data boundary.
# For example, GPT-6.1 Sol via the US geographic profile: modelId="us.openai.gpt-6.1-sol"
# GPT-6 Sol via the US geographic profile: strong reasoning and coding for complex work.
response = bedrock.converse(
    modelId="us.openai.gpt-6-sol",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Summarize recent AI regulatory trends in Canada."}]}],
    inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 512},
)

# GPT-6 Luna via the global profile: fast, low-cost inference for high-volume tasks such as classification.
response = bedrock.converse(
    modelId="global.openai.gpt-6-luna",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Classify this ticket as BILLING, TECHNICAL, or OTHER: ..."}]}],
    inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 256},
)

Tool use

These models support client-side tool use (function calling). Define tools in the tools parameter, and the model returns a structured tool-call request for your application to execute.

response = client.responses.create(
    model="global.openai.gpt-6-astra",
    input="What's the current exchange rate from CAD to USD?",
    tools=[{
        "type": "function",
        "name": "get_exchange_rate",
        "parameters": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "from_currency": {"type": "string"},
                "to_currency": {"type": "string"}
            }
        }
    }],
)

# The model returns a tool-call request rather than text.
for item in response.output:
    if item.type == "function_call":
        print(f"Tool: {item.name}, Args: {item.arguments}")

Prompt caching

GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 support prompt caching on Amazon Bedrock to reduce the cost and latency of repeated prompt prefixes. Implicit caching requires no changes to your code: Amazon Bedrock automatically caches eligible prefixes of 1,024 tokens or more. Cached tokens read on subsequent requests are billed at a discounted rate and do not count against your tokens-per-minute quota. Cached tokens appear in the response usage object and in Amazon CloudWatch metrics so you can track usage. For cache-write pricing, minimum prefix sizes, and support for explicit cache breakpoints, see the prompt caching documentation and the individual model cards.

Quota management

Cross-Region inference quotas on the bedrock-runtime endpoint are measured in tokens per minute (TPM) per model. Each quota combines input and output tokens against a single limit. US geographic and global inference profiles have separate quota allocations, so switching between them changes the pool you draw from.

Token consumption combines input tokens, cache-write input tokens, and output tokens. Output tokens are multiplied by the model’s burndown rate, so output-heavy workloads consume quota faster than raw token counts suggest. Before a production rollout, request quota increases early and monitor quota utilization. Test with representative prompts, output lengths, streaming behavior, concurrency, and peak traffic.

To request a quota increase, follow these steps:

  1. Open the Service Quotas console in ca-central-1 or ca-west-1.
  2. Choose Amazon Bedrock, then select the quota named “Cross-Region InvokeModel tokens per minute” for the model that you need.
  3. Choose Request increase at account level, enter your target value, and submit the request.

For details on how token usage and costs are tracked, see Track usage and costs in Amazon Bedrock.

Observability

Because these models run through the Amazon Bedrock Runtime API, requests made through an inference profile appear in your observability tooling the same way on-demand requests do. Invocation logs and Amazon CloudWatch metrics are recorded in your source Region. This holds regardless of where the request was processed. Your observability stays in one place.

  • AWS CloudTrail logs every request, recording which destination Region served it in the additionalEventData.inferenceRegion field. For example: 
    "additionalEventData": {
  "inferenceProfileArn": "arn:aws:bedrock:ca-central-1:111122223333:inference-profile/global.openai.gpt-6-astra",
  "inferenceRegion": "us-west-2"
}
  • Amazon CloudWatch metrics are published per inference profile, covering invocation count, token count, latency, throttles, and errors.
  • Model invocation logging delivers full request and response payloads to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon CloudWatch Logs. To activate it on the Amazon Bedrock console, choose Settings, then choose Model invocation logging. You can also call the PutModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration API. It is off by default.
  • AWS Data Exports itemizes spend by model and profile.

Amazon CloudWatch Coding Agent Insights

If you use these models to power AI coding assistants such as OpenAI Codex, Amazon CloudWatch Coding Agent Insights provides a dedicated dashboard. It surfaces token usage, API request counts, active users, and cost attribution across dimensions such as department, team, and environment. To activate it, configure your coding agent to export telemetry to Amazon CloudWatch. For the setup steps, see Set up OpenTelemetry for OpenAI Codex.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges after testing, remove the resources you created:

  1. Turn off model invocation logging. On the Amazon Bedrock console, choose Settings, then choose Model invocation logging, or call DeleteModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration. This stops delivery of logs to Amazon S3 and Amazon CloudWatch Logs.
  2. Delete or detach the IAM policies and any Amazon Bedrock API keys that you created for testing.

The inference profiles themselves are system-defined and incur no cost when they aren’t in use.

Security and compliance

Cross-Region inference is designed to protect your data in transit and at rest. Requests travel over the AWS private backbone encrypted with TLS 1.2+ rather than the public internet. For Canadian customers, your data at rest stays in your source Region by default. This includes invocation logs, knowledge bases, and configurations. Only the transient inference computation happens in the destination Region, and by default model providers don’t have access to your prompts or completions.

There’s one consideration specific to OpenAI models. Content flagged by automated abuse classifiers might be retained for up to 30 days in the destination Region for review. If you want to constrain processing to North America (Canada and the US), you can choose the US geographic profile. We recommend reviewing Amazon Bedrock abuse detection with your compliance team.

For a more detailed look at Canadian data residency patterns, see Cross-Region Inference and Canadian Data Residency: A Technical Architecture Guide.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how to access OpenAI GPT-5.6 (Sol, Terra, and Luna), GPT-6 (Astra, Sol, and Luna), and GPT-6.1 Sol from Canada. These models are available from the Canada (Central) and Canada West (Calgary) Regions using cross-Region inference on Amazon Bedrock. We covered the available inference profiles, how to set up permissions and an example SCP, and how to invoke the models with the Responses, Chat Completions, and Converse APIs. For the Responses API, we included streaming and tool-use examples. We also showed how to request quota increases, review usage, and clean up your test resources.

To get started, review the OpenAI model cards in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide, then open the Amazon Bedrock console and send a test prompt through an inference profile. For pricing, see the Amazon Bedrock pricing page.

If you have questions or feedback, leave a comment on this post.

About the authors

Roopesh Ramklass

Roopesh is a Specialist Principal Solutions Architect for AI/ML at AWS, based in Vancouver, Canada, where he helps customers design and scale generative AI solutions. He brings deep expertise across the AI/ML spectrum, partnering with organizations to turn ambitious AI ideas into reliable, high-impact solutions.

Dan MacKay

Dan is the Financial Services Compliance Specialist for AWS Canada. He advises customers on recommended practices and practical solutions for cloud and AI-related governance, risk, and compliance. Dan specializes in helping AWS customers navigate financial services and privacy regulations applicable to the use of cloud and AI technology in Canada with a focus on digital sovereignty, third-party risk management, and operational resilience.

Prasoon Gupta

Prasoon is a Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services (AWS) Canada. He enjoys helping public sector customers modernize and get the most value from the cloud. Outside of work, he enjoys building full-stack, AI-based tools on AWS for fun, spanning serverless architectures, agentic AI, and developer platforms.

Saurabh Trikande

Saurabh is a Senior Product Manager for Amazon Bedrock and Amazon SageMaker Inference. He is passionate about working with customers and partners, motivated by the goal of democratizing AI. He focuses on core challenges related to deploying complex AI applications, inference with multi-tenant models, cost optimizations, and making the deployment of generative AI models more accessible. In his spare time, Saurabh enjoys hiking, learning about innovative technologies, following TechCrunch, and spending time with his family.

Melanie Li

Melanie, PhD, is a Senior Generative AI Specialist Solutions Architect at AWS based in Sydney, Australia, where her focus is on working with customers to build solutions using state-of-the-art AI/ML tools. She has been actively involved in multiple generative AI initiatives across APJ, harnessing the power of LLMs. Prior to joining AWS, Dr. Li held data science roles in the financial and retail industries.

Zohreh Norouzi

Zohreh is a Senior Security Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services (AWS). She helps customers make good security choices and accelerate their journey to the AWS Cloud. She has been actively involved in AI security initiatives, using her expertise to help customers build secure AI solutions at scale.

item.title: Discover tools at runtime with AWS Agent Registry
item.dc:creator: Vibhu Pareek
item.description: Hardcoded tool wiring breaks down as an agent's catalog grows from a handful of tools to hundreds. This post walks through a runtime Discover, Instantiate, Execute loop built on AWS Agent Registry, where an orchestrator discovers MCP servers and A2A agents through semantic search at runtime instead of compiling every tool at build time.
item.content:encoded:
Runtime discovery with AWS Agent Registry can help address a problem that agent demos might hide.
